First of all, yes, I know this game is made for little kids but after everything I experienced in the game (and out), I can not give this game a positive review.
The vehicles in the game, while varied, all feel awkward in the worst ways. Cars grip the road too tightly (and wheels clip through the floor), Boats are way too floaty making challenges involving them much harder than necessary, and Planes move fairly well with a controller but makes weapon powerups mostly useless.
Powerups in the game in general are a mix of too weak or overpowered. Each powerup is the usual Mario Kart-esque powerups you tend to see in kart racers, green shells, mushrooms, bullet bill, banana, and lightning bolt. The Lightening Bolt, Shells, and Banana powers are fairly weak and don't help give as much of an advantage as the speed boosts given by the other items and on a 3d plane with the... plane, dodging non-homing weapons is too easy making those powerups completely useless.
The game also offers controller compatibility, well, kind of. To use controller, you must turn on Gamepad controls in the settings, the issue with this is that the controller works in races but barely works on the menu screens, sometimes working, sometimes half working, sometimes not at all. The bigger issue with this is the fact that the game looks like it might have been ported almost directly from a console version as all the menu's show Wii-esque "Press B to go back"  messages. Feels like a lazy port to me especially when my first completion of a tour was not actually saved in the game.
Stages are also a concern in my opinion. For a kid's kart racer there are a lot of twists and turns which is not a concern to me but the fact that they had the chance to use nice popping colors for a Hello Kity but instead make everything look bland, and in one case hard to tell which was the race path, an opportunity was missed there. Another missed opportunity is the fact that one of the first stages has a waterfall that pushes everyone towards a wall to show off the possibility of physics in the game, albeit it is not very clear that the waterfall is doing it and it just feels like the rocks are magnetized, they don't ever use the physics creatively again. Even the ice in winter levels doesn't feel like ice. Also there are again issues with clipping everywhere, the cars in general tends to clip their wheels through the ground but most starting lines and speed boost pads float above the ground.
The difficulty curves based on tours in the game, or rather that is what it is supposed to do. Each tour is like the next step in difficult AI drivers. Problem is that the final tour which should be the hardest ended up being the easiest due to glitches. On 1 stage, one of the AI continuously drove in circles near the finish line which also was a map with very hard to dodge iceberg obstacles but what was worse was that on another stage, the road had a very large invisible wall that stopped every racer, once you figure out where the invisible wall ends, the final race of the game ....is against no one. I finished the entire race before any of the AI finished 1 lap because they were trapped.
And my final complaint about this game...
I uploaded 7+ screenshots of my gameplay. Of these screenshots, the 3 screenshots of actual in game gameplay and not just Huds/Menus were flagged by Valve and caused me to receive a 3 day ban from posting to the community. Hello Kitty screenshots got me temprarily banned from uploading screenshots.
This game is not worth even $5.
P.S. There is no button to exit the game.

Before I get into why I have given this a negative review, let me just say that the core gameplay is solid. I like the mission system they have going on, and the cards are cool and (for the most part) balanced. If you enjoy TCG's (If you dont why are you even reading this? :P) you will almost certinatly get a good few hours out of this game, unlocking new cards and seeing a visible increase in your power. If your looking for something to play on the side, this could well be the game for you. And hey, its free, so dont just take my words for it, go and give it a try yourself, you have literally nothing to loose.
-------
Unfortunatly I dont think this game is really worth the time anymore. As someone with limited funds this was a great TCG with some interesting mechanics, and (imo) none of the cheese that Hearthstone has.
That is still the case, however the rate at which you earn in-game money (to buy new packs) has become so incredably slow that in order to compete you will have to open your wallet every time a new batch of cards comes along just to stay competative, and even then the random nature of TCG packs means even if you spend money, your not guarenteed the cards your actually looking for. The way around this is to buy Premium Packs which guarentee you copies of cards you dont yet have a playset (4 copies) for. At lower levels they are basically money down the drain compared to regular packs, at higher levels/when you have most cards it seems to me that the only real way to get the cards your looking for is to buy those packs.
That being said, there is a crafting system of sorts where you can dissasemble cards you dont want/already have a playset  of in order to earn "Mana" cards, which you can then spend on unlocking cards you need. Great system in all honesty, but it all comes down to the grind, which is simply no fun. The prices for the higher tier cards are quite simply rediculous.
The new cards added feel... well... cheaty(?) compared to the old and in general not incredably well balenced, this leads to even the AI roflstomping your until-2-days-ago pretty sweet deck youve spent ages crafting into oblivion. Not to mention the unlockable heros being rediculously overpowered compared to the free starter ones. Adding in the Hero Packs was and is a brilliant idea, but again, they cost far to much for what you earn in-game.
The mission system is good, like I said in the beginning, but again, rewards are far to low to really make them worth doing anymore.
At its core I do NOT feel that this is a p2w game, but at higher levels it seems to be slipping in that direction.
All TCG's have a p2w element, which I think everybody expects before even getting into them, and I have taken that into account but its got to the point where I feel im being pushed to pay rather than play, and thats no fun.
After 200 hours in the game this is one that im going to have to leave to the side and only play on occasion if im bored. Its a huge shame, if they up the rewards for matches then maybe I will get back into it, but for now, its a no, and that makes me sad :(

This was not the kind of game I was expecting. It's very much focused on your "family" of assassins and your connections to them. You're trying to solve a mystery, but you're forced to go on these assignments that have nothing to do with what's going on.
Pros:
-Story was long enough.
-Opportunities to increase your stats, more often than similar games.
-There was one interesting fight, but I don't want to give spoilers. You can choose to romance this person as well, which I thought was pretty cool and went well with my character.
-The reason 'why' part of the mystery was a twist I wasn't expecting. But the 'how' I saw coming a mile away.
Neutral:
-Tries really hard to give you romance options.
-What you did will give you the ending of the story, don't have the option to choose.
-Ending will take into account reputation, fame, money, character fates.
-Secrets and hidden achievements.
Cons:
-The writing is pretty bad, I found alot of it silly and ridiculous.
-Alot of the time the game ignores your abilities and decisions. A scene just plays out with you dropping bodies like you're a super assassin. You always accomplish your mission.
-Spend alot of time hanging out with your assassin friends and descibing the beauty around you, rather than focusing on how you're going to complete your mission.
-Way too many characters, very one dimensional archetypes, didn't care about most of them, they're boring. You meet a bunch of characters then next chapter a new bunch of characters are introduced. How many assassins are there?!?
-Didn't like the references to previous missions you haven't gone on. Makes you feel like you're missing a part of the story.
-Disappointing final boss fight.
Final Verdict:
Game tried really hard to make you a team player who cares about their "family". You may find the story more engaging if you play your character this way, and not a lone wolf like I did. If you like the story there's certainly good replay options. But for me it just wasn't worth the time or money, this is one of the weaker CYOA games.

This is another one of those choose-your-own-adventure type text-based games in the same basic style (but not of the same quality) as Choice of Robots, Choice of Alexandria or Champion of the Gods. It features the same huge flaw; the inability to simply turn the page back to a previous choice or a previous page.
I have to admit though, on my first play through I was very impressed with this game. It's campy and silly and purposefully cliched in many of the right ways. The descriptions are good and visceral but the writing style never takes itself seriously as it is continually heavy-handed. In a way, this is a very well-done parody of those dime-a-dozen thriller novels featuring assassins and murder-for-hire secret organizations and so forth. The choices seem interesting and it feels as though each choice may be very important and could potentially lead to a very different conclusion. Unfortunately any sense of choice this game provides is largely an illusion.
I started to see some serious draw-backs to this game during my second and third times through. Some choices seem to have fairly arbitrary results and all choices ultimately lead you either to the exact same death paragraph or the exact same final battle encounter. Some paragraphs are swapped in or out in favor of others depending on how evil your character is or depending on which side characters you've chosen to support along the way but the story is, very unfortunately, largely the same no matter what you do, unless you act extremely stupidly and manage to die before the story's end.
Worse still, despite the initially compelling sense of danger this game provides, this game is actually extremely forgiving, particularly given its subject matter. Situations in which you should instantly die merely cause you to be wounded and you will usually have the opportunity to get healed before the next chapter. Once, I literally played through the game trying to get my character killed and didn't manage it until well into the second half of this game's story, mostly because I refused to allow him to get healed whenever the opportunity to do so presented itself.
From the standpoint of being challenged to find the right path to a successful ending of some kind, this game practically plays itself and worst of all, you get pretty much the same ending (only with different moral overtones) no matter what choices you make. There is a single juncture at which you can either choose to end the game or continue but that is almost the only real decision that really seems to matter so far as changing the story's ultimate ending. The potential have the amazing experience of peering into a myriad of radically altered versions of the future, each based on your different potential choices, a trait which should ideally be common to all choose-your-own-adventure type games/stories, is largely ignored here.
There is no way, for example, to choose to side with the story's antagonists. There is no way to try to escape the confines of the story's plot and lead a life that is irrelevant to being an assassin (you can't drop everything and become a used car salesman instead). There is no way to simply♥♥♥♥♥♥around and do nothing until you get killed. The game forces you to go on airplane flights, to take certain missions, to go to Miami. Even if you fail all your early assassination missions, the game's final confrontation will still happen where it always does. No matter what skills you emphasize along the way, if you win, the villain will still be brought down in a very similar way (during a kung fu fight). This game offers few true choices. Playing it more than once merely kills your time.

It's straight forward. The writing could definitely be better, as there aren't too many elements about any characters, or the story on the whole that I would write home about. It’s fairly predictable, and it’s very easy to navigate the game with a single set of skills without issue or conflict.
But with the stream of mediocre and even poor games released from Choice of Games, it was nice to play something that was straight forward. The game was advertised as one where you get to be an assassin, and it delivers on that front. That seems like an oddly simple thing to praise a game for, but that’s exactly where these games have been failing of late. They’ve been so busy preaching its own morality that it stopped feeling like I was embarking on an adventure of my own will. They’ve been taking place in entirely author created worlds with too many moving pieces and not nearly enough words or time to let the reader immerse themselves into it; that too with worlds that aren’t nearly as interesting as the respective authors believe them to be. They’re so distracted at being something else that they stop being choose your own adventures.
This was just that, an adventure where you’re choosing the details, and steering the story. It’s not one of the truly better Choice of Games entries, but I have to give it a positive review for having the right idea, when others are trending in a worse direction. It's another CCG like magic the gathering, but unlike magic, this one has some minor differences like creature speed (slower creatures can't block faster ones etc.) and creatures can attack other creatures. The mechanics are what you'd expect more or less with a few added twists here and there.
The best feature has to be the mana system. Every card has a mana cost and an aspect level cost. With mana cards you can either get a level in the aspect or +1 mana and +1 card. If you don't have a mana card in your hand, you can shuffle an unwanted card into your library and get a mana card if it's in the first five top cards. This makes the game way less dependant on luck, and you almost never get mana screwed.
The art style is great, each aspect has their own unique mechanics and creature types, and there are of course fun decks to build by mixing them. The graphics are a bit bare bones, the effects cards make are nothing special, and there's only one battlefield, but it's fine.
The best reason to play this game is it's free to play model. There's a map screen with quests like, play 3 games, win 5 games, gain X fame, beat an obnoxiously difficult AI opponent, etc. You have to unlock the questing site first (this serves as a form of a tutorial, you have to play with decks of a certain aspect in order to unlock the quest site). After that's done, every day you can choose one of few quests to do with rewards like gold, uncommon cards, foil cards, rate cards, trial tickets, and even premium currency. And the you even get boosters and hero packs for free when you level up along with gold. They really shower you with gifts, and I have pretty much every card released for free just by paying the game.
Multilayer is also cool with trials (draft) and tournaments every day.
There's nothing in the premium currency shop that you can't get by just playing except card backs which don't impact the gameplay. Premium currency is just to sued things up if you want, but getting cards is already fast and if you need specific cards you can craft them, and covert excess copies of cards into crafting material (and you craft cards with mana shrines).
You'll never feel obligated to buy something to progress, even without spending any money it's possible to win multiplayer.
The only thing you have to pay for if you want access to it is the single player campaign. But you get tons of cards from it so you still don't lose anything should you choose to buy it, you're basically buying cards with it along with the experience.
All in all a pretty generous game with fun mechanics. Nothing groundbreaking, but has a nice active community and fun gameplay.

This is easily among my favorite, if not being my absolute favorite, of the interactive novels presented by Choice of Games/Hosted Games. If the alluring fantasy of being a sleek, cool assassin in fiction has ever appealed to you, whether it's through playing Hitman, The Darkness, or taking on the Dark Brotherhood quests in the Elder Scrolls series, or being enthralled by movies like John Wick and Pulp Fiction, this game is for you.
The writing does a great job of making your character feel formidable and impressive, and rewards how you want to personally characterize them from their personality to their skill set with a rich and interesting set of possibilities. It's one of the closest and most rewarding things I've found outside of some other conventional video games that lets you more or less live out what it would be like to be the star in a high octane action film.
I would freely encourage anyone who thinks they might be interested to check out COG's other games/novels as well (all the free demos let you play out the first three chapters, giving you a fair taste of whether it'll hold your interest or not, so you can't really go wrong there), as I've found most of them to be pretty enjoyable, but I can definitely say there's probably nothing else they can offer that's quite like this.
Of course, the story isn't 100% realistic, but where's the fun in that? If you can suspend your disbelief enough for an interactive novel the same way you would for 1980's Bruce Willis and Arnold Schwarzenegger movies, but don't want a story that's completely mindless or unbelievable, give the demo a shot at the very least (no pun intended). Not many of their games are usually $5 on Steam, but I'd say this is one of the instances where it's definitely worth it.
The first time I beat this game, I immediately started another playthrough. This is one I can definitely see myself coming back to again and again over time. It'd be a mistake not to try it if you think you might even be the least bit interested.

+ Deep strategy layer that forces you to adapt to different situations
+ Beatiful graphics for environment, units, spells and rage spirits

Cons

Are you kidding? "It's Killing Time" is so bad, it's funny. I was actually laughing out loud at how much more ridiculous the story got with each passing chapter. It's hard to explain without revealing any spoilers. But that's part of the problem. The story is so poorly written, it drops spoilers on itself. Predictable is too mild a word. The characters are so 1-dimensional, that you can just match them up with their 'Creative Writing 101' archetype when they are introduced. At first there was disappointment with these flaws. But about half way thru, the story reached a point of absurdity that I couldn't help smiling at how awful it was. I also couldn't help but use the 'vast power of my imagination' to envision the author asking himself - "How big a turd will these Choice of Games people pay me to pop out?" The big twist is beyond telegraphed. It's like when a little kid tries to whisper something to you and its louder than if he had spoken in his normal voice. And this so-called twist is delivered to you by a character that is even too campy to be a Bond villain - it's all just laughable! This is the kind of game you gift to someone as a practical joke. I am seriously asking - was this *meant* to be funny? I can't tell.
But I feel kind of guilty wondering if it may have been a genuine effort at entertaining people. Oh ... that's sad. Now I feel bad again. To avoid inflicting upon others the crushing sense of despair that comes from realizing someone might have poured their heart and soul into something so dreadful, I can't recommend this story/game to anyone. Advice for the Choice of Games people - replace 'ultra-violent' with 'ultra-hilarious' in the game description and repackage it as an assassin parody- but don't tell the author. Then I will come back and give the game a thumbs up.
Now I guess I'll go take a magic healing bubble bath that can help cure gunshot wounds, just like the hero of the story does after a tough mission. I'm not kidding. It's just that ridiculous.

I really love this game. It's like the missions where you don't have a castle in Heroes of Might and Magic games, only much more fun. It takes place in a fantasy world that seems generic at first, but a healthy dose of humor and irony (and bad translations from Russian) set it apart from the rest. And some quests and artifacts you'll encounter are definitely not generic!
Gameplay-wise, you'll be mostly wandering around beautifully detailed areas, collecting loot, avoiding high-level baddies and looking for fights you can take on so you can level up, and so on. The fights themselves are a beautiful tactical affair, you're always trying to minimize losses and to make the best of troops you can hire locally (some people insist on making long back and forth trips to replenish troops instead of working with what they have, I think it's a fun-killer). There area many spells and special abilities to spice things up.
The only criticism I would have is that later areas of the game can be very difficult especially if you didn't make a very good character build, and there are less fun quests to lighten things up. Latter areas are also less well-designed. Overall though, you have a lot of liberty for the order in which you want to tackle the late game challenges, and finishing the game was satisfying despite having taken two year-long breaks.
Highly recommended!

2.) Travel all the way back across the world to get your 40 extra archers.
3.) Travel all the way back across the world to get to the next quest.
4.) Fight the next quest and either lose some troops or level up (and get capacity for more troops).  Now you're at 90 / 120 archers.
5.) Travel all the way back across the world only to find that there are no more archers to hire.
There is some fun to be had with the game, but you'll spend 2/3 of your playtime shuttling troops to-and-fro instead of actually playing the game.  Mechanics like this make me not recommend the game... but if you have the stomach for this kind of thing then you could pick it up and have some fun.

I have a hard time recommending this game because the core game is so good, and everything surrounding it is awful. With that said, I still DO recommend it, but keep in mind what you're getting into:
Pros:
- Gameplay. The entire concept of the game and the mechanics are flawless. If you like fast-paced, skill-based competitive games, you will like Nidhogg.
Cons:
- Awful menus. Seriously, the buttons you use to navigate make no sense. This is even worse in online mode, where you have to use his built-in chat. Using Shift+Tab to try to chat with Steam (or losing focus from the Nidhogg window in ANY way, usually) results in a disconnect.
- Lack of "variant" options in online play. The Boomerang Swords variant is amazing and you can't use it online. It's very disappointing.
- Netcode sucks. Dev should have just implemented GGPO. Nidhogg is basically a fighting game, and MikeZ pointed out in his talk at UFGTX that everyone should be using GGPO for their fighting game netcode because it's cheap enough and works incredibly well.
- No Linux support even though it's made with Game Maker.
- Zero dev support. This is the worst part of it all, really. There have only been 4 maps since the game's release. The dev is aware of the fact that people love this game and is not investing any time in giving us either more maps, or better yet, Steam Workshop support for custom maps. This game is $15, and that's a lot for the technical complexity (or lack thereof) in this game. We're paying him more for the fact that this game is a really novel idea with well-executed gameplay, and it'd be nice to play on more than 4 maps.
All in all, is it worth the buy? Yes, if and only if you have friends who will play LOCALLY with you. Not online. Though you might want to wait for a sale. You'll quickly find yourself getting bored with 4 maps, as my friends and I did, and it's really unfortunate, but that's just how it is.

Despite being able to overly simplify this game's main story, the dialogue, texts, and overall rich detail lets you know a lot of thought went into this game's lore. You realize that events have occurred prior to the start of this game and that isn't always the case with video games. It's almost as if the past is just as important as the present in this game.

Honestly, this is all apparent as you play through the game, but at times its approach requires you to actively seek out texts/knowledge of the game's lore. This isn't too appealing to me, I'd rather just concentrate on the gameplay and if something stood out to me, I'd look it up online. Who knows, maybe this is something you're interested in so it'll just contribute to your overall enjoyment of this game, but if it doesn't, the game is diverse enough to keep you entertained.

The level design in this game is noteworthy because very few of them look the same, they're all more or less interconnected and they all offer a unique experience that greatly differs from what has been previously encountered. What's also great about them is the different background music that's played depending on which area you're in. Some games have problems with this by having music that's either too repetitive or intrusive. The thing about this music is that besides being diverse, it's not distracting or boring, it just adds to the overall experience.

One thing that's almost immediately noticeable about VSAC is the amount of variety that's offered. Not only with the level design, but with the combat, magic system, enemies, and music. All of this is done in such a way that you can tell a lot of thought went into this game. I'm not exactly sure of what the other playable characters are capable of, due to having only played with the warrior class, but even with that one character there's a lot of possibilities.

With the warrior class, your attacks primarily consists of sword combat that is easy to utilize, but difficult to master. The combat is difficult to master because it's combo based and it's to your advantage to create long chains of attacks. Not all combos you learn will work against every enemy you encounter so It takes a bit of practice/creativity, but the longer/more diverse your combos are, the more damage you will inflict.  At the same time, trying to keep combos in mind isn't always possible. At times, the combat becomes quite hectic and you will more or less end up button mashing in an attempt to overcome the situation at hand or you'll stick to the combos that you feel work best, it can sometimes be repetitive.

Besides the basic sword attacks, you also have around five different types of magic that each consist of four individual spells. For the most part, this magic is used to heal, damage, and help you navigate through specific areas of the game. It may sound odd, but the usage of magic really helps when you're playing as the warrior character. I endlessly found myself in situations where I had to rely on my spells to heal myself and it was invaluable when used as part of my combos against enemies.

At this point I'm sure that I've already mentioned how this game has variety in more ways than one, but this is also showcased through the enemies/bosses you encounter. Boss battles are an important part of this game and you will encounter many as you progress through it. It's important to note that alongside being numerous, the bosses are also diverse. There are a slight amount of bosses that require you to beat them more than once, but they are all different. Not only through their appearance, but also with their attack patterns/damage they deal. Their attack patterns are important because through memorizing them, it's how you determine the best way to beat the bosses.

The difficult boss battles weren't the only things that bothered me. Despite being a great game, it's not perfect and I have a few complaints about it. I keep repeating myself by stating how diverse/variety filled this game is, but at times this variety isn't really useful. The game has an item/crafting system, but overall it seems unnecessary. You can go through most of the game without needing extra items or armor and it's only in extreme situations that you need to upgrade your gear/purchase something. I feel that it's not as useful as it could be because most of the necessary items can be picked up/found as you traverse the many locations found in this game and your playstyle can make having to upgrade your equipment unnecessary.

Speaking of many locations, there's a lot to see/visit in this game. The problem with that is how once you're done with these levels, you'll still need to visit them because they are sometimes connected to other areas. My problem with this is that there's no real fast travel system. There's a tram system that will allow you to travel to the three main "towns" found in the game, but within those towns there are other areas that aren't always near the tram system. It can get annoying having to travel long distances from location to location and it's not always easy. It's not easy to travel because the game lacks a large world map and it only has a map of the specific area you're currently in. If the game had a large world map, I'm sure it would've been easier to locate/travel to the areas where you needed to be.

A continuation of the previously mentioned problem is not being clearly told what your objectives require of you. The game regularly updates a small message found within the map screen that lets you know what your current objective is, but the problem is that for this main objective to be completed, you will unknowingly have two or more smaller objectives to deal with. This can be problematic because it leads to a lot of back tracking that will just result in lost time until you figure out what you need to do.

One positive that can arise from the endless backtracking in this game is discovering how many optional areas there are. They're done in such a way that it doesn't feel like a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt to add more playtime to the game. At the same time, I feel as if the inclusion of these optional areas can be problematic. Like most of the other areas found in this game, they consist of many enemies/bosses to kill. While this can be viewed as a good thing because it'll lead to leveling up/finding rare items, I feel as if it's counterintuitive due to there being a low max level. I know that there has to be a max level because endless leveling up isn't possible, but with the many possibilities for grinding, you'd think the max level would harder to reach.

I previously mentioned that this game's character animations are quite fluid, but this really isn't the case with all of the game's controls and they're not as smooth as they can be. Being a 2D metroidvania, you can expect for there to be quite a bit of platforming and by its very definition this will consist of a lot of jumping. However, in this game it lacks mobility and if timed incorrectly, it could lead to damage or unintentionally landing elsewhere.
Along with the jumping, the dashing also wasn't as smooth as it could be. Maybe the game's designer(s) wanted to do something different, but other games have done a better job with the dashing mechanic. Most games will consist of rapidly pressing down twice in the direction you wish to dash, but in VSAC you either press down + the direction you want to dash to or precisely press down on the left/right+ down at the same time.

Overall, I enjoyed VSAC and recommend it. My complaints towards it aren't awful and while slightly taking away from the experience, they don't make the game unplayable, it's still a worthwhile experience.

Great game with lots of potential to be the premiere tavern/adventurer management game.
You are a tavern owner and it's your job to keep the drinks flowing, the food served, all while managing adventurers that you hire on to do quests. Your tavern is small in the beginning, and as your adventurers complete quests and share the profits as they return, you will eventually be able to upgrade your tavern with all kinds of upgrades. These can be aesthetic upgrades, like changing wall colors, adding furniture, upgrading your rooms to more pleasing ones, getting better drinks or food, or even things like a Blacksmith to produce better equipment for your adventurers. On top of that you need to keep the booze and food stocked so managing your funds is important.
Adventurers level up over time, and each adventurer has their own unique story and background, as well as a variety of classes that allow for some fantastic party combinations full of fun and interesting dialogue as they quest. Some adventurers are better suited for certain quests so you won't always want to take the same adventurers out questing.
There's a lot of management windows which show you your tavern income, and various other expeditures for those who want to run numbers.
There's still a few bugs due to the Early Access release, however the devs are on top of them smashing them with their +1 hammers. There's also a lot more content to be added so its at the very beginning stages of Early Access, even though there's quite a bit of content there already.
If you love this type of genre then the price point shouldn't be a problem for you. But if you want a fully finished product, then you may want to add this to your wishlist and wait a few months and see how the development goes.

Valdis Story is an indie metrodvania with hack n slash combat and RPG elements, very much in the style of 16bit and 32 bit classics.  Meh, doesn't sound like much to write home about?  Well the game may not be winning any prizes for being  orginal, but it is done so well that even some of its considerable flaws don't hold this back from being an absolute tour de force
+ Amazing music that perfectly combines with the tone of the levels, from sombre symphonic pieces in the down time to raging children of bodom style metal when the poop hits the fan
+ beautiful and very strong art style,that eschews the common pixel art in favour of a bold and colorful style thats somewhere between a watercolour painting and the moomin, if the moomin were in fantasy hack n slash land.  Also lovely fluid animations
+ stastifying RPG elemts which allow you to experiment with stats, modifiers, spells, weapons and skills to build your character the way you want.
+ chunky hack n slash combat
+ VERY WELL optomised - runs at 60fps on my ancient 4gb laptop (GT420m)
+ good story
+ interesting level design and plenty of secrets and optional areas
+ high replay value with a choice of (eventually) 4 main characters, each with different playstyles
However:
- a bit too much backtracking
- sometimes groups enemies will juggle/stunlock you for what feels like an eternity
- do i really need to do a hadouken on the d-pad to dodge?
- the controls often feel a bit 'sticky' and unresponsive. While the combat seems to work ok, the platforming sections really need precision, especially in cases where you have timed unlocking doors which need to be activated in complex sequences, and the game doesn't deliver.  As that crestfallen♥♥♥♥♥♥Hawkwood would say, 'it gives me conniptions'
despite these criticisms, and the controls are a fairly major one in my view, they don't hold Valdis back from being a stunningly great game, one that i really did enjoy and would recommend to any fan of the genre.  But, you might wanna check out the free demo first  - dem sticky controls gonna drive some people up the wall!

You're the guardian angel of a family, a skeleton in a wardrobe that somehow nobody notices.  When the family moves to a new house and leaves you behind, possibly because they don't know you exist, you have to find a way to rejoin them.  The artwork is great, every room is full of video game and pop culture references, and your protagonist, Skinny the Skeleton, continuously breaks the fourth wall, cracking wise about about the actions you instruct him to take.  He even insults you for trying nonsensical stuff like illogical combinations of inventory items.  What Skinny doesn't do, unfortunately, is provide the player with enough clues.  I love point-and-click adventures.  I hate having to use a walkthrough.  This game made me do that a lot, and not once did I think, "Oh, I should have figured that one out."  Okay, maybe there was *one* thing I should have figured out on my own, but the rest?  Even the walkthrough writer comments after one puzzle solution: "I have no idea why this works."  As previously mentioned, Skinny insults you when you try illogical actions, and sometimes says, "Using everything in you inventory on everything else isn't how you win this game."  That, however, is a big fat lie.  Trying everything in your inventory on everything in the game is the only way to finish it, as a number of the puzzles and their solutions make no sense whatsoever.  None.  How long is this game?  A little north of an hour if you use the walkthrough all the way; six to eight hours if you do your best to figure things out and resort to a walkthrough only when you're really stuck; without use of a walkthrough at all?  I dunno. Decades.  I give this game a thumbs up for the style, appearance, UI, story, and some excellent humour.  It gets a thumbs down for some of the puzzles, and another twitch of the thumbs down for  a couple of the voice actors.  Most of the voice acting is good, so the bad ones really stand out.  Play this game with a walkthrough handy, and don't feel guilty about it, since some of the puzzles are so obtuse, even Steve Meretzky would be scratching his head.

Don't play this game unless you're willing to pay for it. Yes, you can get everything for free, but the grinding necessary is relentless. Of course it is. These kinds of games only exist to make money, and besides, they need to pay for the servers, and the people who programmed this game.
I would recommend it if you're willing to buy everything, but not if you want to play for free. Besides, if you do want to play a ccg for free, there are genuinely free alternatives out there. I can name one that requires far less grinding than this game, as in you actually feel like you're making progress (and there is no way to 'buy' anything in the game anyway, though you can donate to support the game) but I doubt I would be allowed to mention another game on here.
I'm rating this as 'no' just because I have to choose an option. Like I said, whether or not you should play this game depends on whether you have the money for it or not.
edit: I decided that perhaps I should talk about what this game is. Its essentially just a slight modification of Magic: the gathering. The differences are rather few. The most obvious is that you can attack your opponent's creatures directly. You also get to draw a card every time you play a mana (unless you use it to build a 'level', cards have both a mana cost and a minimum level to play them). Also, there's a feature that lets you look at the top 5 cards of your deck, once per turn, and take out a mana you see and put it into your hand (you then have to shuffle the cards onto the bottom of your deck). This feature is rather handy, but it can be devastating if it misses, especcially since you have to remove a card from your hand to pay for the ability. So you do lose something if the ability misses, but it does hit often enough where using the ability is worth it, despite the risk. But if you're screwed if you don't get a mana, and the ability misses, often times you may as well concede its so devastating.
The game isn't technically bad, the problem is I don't think it really deserves the 'free to play' tag. But then again, most f2p games don't.

This review is for singleplayer only.
Not being a fan or even understanding Warhammer 40K here, I found the game to be a little over the top but still really fun to play. The story isn't great, but maybe I'm lacking context. Either way it's about the gameplay, it is a game after all. This being my first RTS type game I chose the "EASY" difficulty. Missions have different objectives and make the same-ish gameplay level to level very enjoyable despite feeling similar in the core mechanics. There's an epic boss every stage or so and for the most part they're fair challenges. This isn't a simple run-and-gun game even on easy, you have to think about a plan of attack and strategize, figuring out how to take on each presented encounter with an enemy.
This is a squad-based RTS and I thinik it fits the theme really well. You're an awesome space marine commander! The amount of customization you can give to each squad is deep enough to deserve some attention. No you can't change their cosmetics beyond armor stlye but that's not really the point. The RPG elements in this game definitely add a layer of complexity but also provide reason for going back and doing an optional mission. You'll gain XP and maybe find some rare gear for your squads!
TL;DR: This is an RTS in an established series, offering hardcore fans of the series another game to enjoy and offering new players (like me) a very good experience.

I really wish there was a way to present a sort of middle of the road review, but whatever.  So I really am enjoying this idle game, but there are a number of things I wish it did better. Overall, the game isn't bad, but you could simply play the game directly from the website rather than Steam and the battles really need to be a little more fine-tuned.

King's Bounty: The Legend is a solid HOMM-like RPG game that offers a lot of content in a small package. The strategic battles are the highlight of the game and you will spend most of your time battling. While the battles are great, they can be tiresome if you wind up binge playing the game - and you will because it is addictive. The graphics have aged decently and the use of bright, vivid colors keeps the game looking fresh, although textures on character models are clearly dated.
Trying to avoid enemies on the map can be frustrating at times if you want to skip some unnecessary battles, you'll do well to use the arrows on the keyboard to control your character because using the mouse will sometimes catapult you right in front of the enemy.
The gameplay and slow character progression are what will keep bringing you back to play the game, although the story is threadbare and woven through mostly uninteresting, cliched text dialogues. The main character's seemingly witty and satiric retorts during dialogues often made me cringe.
The soundtrack overall is okay, though I was definitely tired of listening to the same music by the end of the game. If you do most of the sidequests, you can expect 50+ hours of gameplay. I played a warrior but I really liked using some of the stronger spells, I will play a mage in one of the sequels after a long break from the King's Bounty series.

Unique, cute and awkward 'choose your own ending' visual novel - but with a much better (IMO) style and user experience than the typical visual novel type game. The animations/illustrations are very good, well done with believable and responsive actions from the female character - although it's drawn, the characters and objects you interact with feel 'realistic'. The characters are as personable as they could be in a 'morning after' interaction so, whilst things are certainly awkward (as they would be IRL in that situation), following certain paths in the conversation enables you to get some interesting information about the woman and to start to develop a real-feeling connection with her. In general, the whole concept is interesting, and this game does make you think a bit about a situation you may/may not have been in IRL and about human relationships more generally.
The game is however pretty short and repetitive if you're doing it several times over - in the end, I just wanted to get all the achievements so I found myself skipping through most of the dialogue to try out different combinations of answers and find all the endings. Even doing that, I've only managed to accumulate a couple hours of play time, and I think if you're just having a look at this for fun it'll probably only occupy you for half an hour/an hour. Mind, if you do take your time to try find every ending though there is a great plot twist revealed which completely changes the way you look at the situation you were just in (or at least it did for me!).
tl;dr Intersting concept well executed. Won't keep you busy for long but if you have a couple quid to spare it's pretty unique and worth having a look around

-- Micro --
At it's core, it's a platformer/beat-em-up like the MegaMan X series. But more close-range focus, so think more like MegaMan Zero.
Unlike MegaMan Zero's combat though, there's a much greater attention to detail on the skill needed to kill enemies. With a significantly higher time-to-kill and much more complicated movesets, individual enemies pose a significant threat. Contrast this to MegaMan where you just plow through everything.
A few aspects of combat are taken from 2D competitive fighters. Not the bad ones like obnoxious input requirements and absurdly long movelists. But the good aspects like balancing offense with defense, applying pressure, knowing when you need to back off, and seeing when an opening presents itself. This tactical mind-game feeling starts to kick in once you get out of the first starter area (or earlier if you crank up the difficulty).
--Macro--
At a larger scale, it's an exploration and backtrack game like Super Metroid. But with better shortcuts for already explored areas and with denser content, so think more like Metroid Fusion. But also with clearer direction on your current high-level goal, so think about some Metroid Prime as well.
Besides wailing on dudes in platforming action, there's also some platforming puzzles and timed elements to challenege your skills. Some are required, a lot are optional. A good rule of thumb is that if it seems really difficult, it's probably an optional one.
There is one particular failure point late into the final part of the game where you're told to get 2 items, but aren't told where they are, that are really out in the middle of nowhere. There's another point earlier in the game that has a key item that's possible to miss on your way through an area, and you'll bumble about trying to find it for a bit if you miss it. In general though, the game is pretty good about keeping you going in the right direction. But if you ever get stuck wondering where to go in these few cases: check a map online, it won't harm your enjoyment of the game.
--Meta--
There's multiple characters (2 at start, 2 unlocked), that play really differently from each other. There's lot of items/gear/talents and whatnot to customize your playstyle even further.
You can also find health extensions (like MegaMan/Metroid sub-tanks), but the game's beatable without them. In fact, boss battles give you a ranking after you beat them, and if you didn't take enough damage to trigger a sub-tank refilling your health, then you get a better score.
In general, there's a very wide difficulty band. Beyond the base difficulty level you select at start, there's a lot of ways that you personally can make the game easier or more difficult as you play through it. Set your own challeneges and push yourself to overcome them. Even with all this versatilitiy, the core difficulty curve is pretty smooth throughout the game, so you don't encounter crazy difficulty spikes. That said, it ramps up to a higher final difficulty level relative to it's starting point than most platformers, so you might want to be careful about cranking up the difficulty on starting a new game if you're not prepared to take a few savage beat-downs.
-- Overall --
Anyone that's looking to make a 2D platformer/beat-em-up with a Metroid-like structure should use this game as a key reference point. If you're looking to make more of a 2D platformer/shooter +Metroid, then reference Shadow Complex.

Once upon a time (in 1998) there was a game called Thief.
Thief was one of the first games  that actually had stealth as a main gameplay mechanic.
In the same year we were also treated with a game called "Metal Gear Solid" on Playstation (1).
Styx reminds me of those games in many respects, and you know what, thats a good thing.
So where are we ?
Remember the game "Of Orcs and Men" ?
Well, we are in the exact same world and we find ourselves in the labyrinthian Atrium of Akenash.
A behemoth of a tower that was build by the technocratic human empire to encapsulate the magical Tree of Life.
In this world humanity is an imperial race with a knack for technology.
Their world views however are fascistic in nature.
Humanity considers itself superior to all other races, and Elves, Orcs and Goblins are all persecuted or enslaved.
We see this world through the eyes of Styx, a cynical Goblin, who is after the Tree of Life and the devine powers it is said to have.
Styx however is a Goblin, which means he is small, and not very bulky, so don't expect a warhammer wielding tank type character here.
Styx however has other tricks up his sleeve, and this is where the game gets interesting.
Since we already established that Styx isn't a bulky fighter, he has to think of other ways to defeat his enemies.
Now Styx happens to be very agile, meaning he can use the environment to his advantage, and boy, does this game offer you a lot of options in this regard !
With the Atrium of Akenash being riddled with all kinds of hallways, tunnels, hidden passages you can approach every single situation in at least 3 different ways.
If you start throwing Styx's more magical abilities into the mix, things get even more interesting.
This is where the game shines.
A well planned takedown feels rewarding and using your magical abilities and the environment is fun.
Being a successful pickpocket is also good fun.
Styx also evolves throughout the course of the game as several new skills are learned in different skill trees.
These RPG elements add another layer to the gameplay, and you can build Styx in many different ways, suiting your playstyle.
This means that my Styx characterbuild can be very different from yours, each with its own pros or cons.
Your inventory is very limited. This means you really have to take care with using your resources, since they can't always be replenished.
How refreshing !
Combat is hard in this game.
Basically all of your opponents are bigger, well armed and stronger than you.
So don't expect fancy swordplay and enemies waiting in line for you to hack them down like in Assassins Creed.
Styx is lethal to the unsuspecting opponent, and has a good chance in a one on one combat situation, but facing more than one opponent at the same time, is doomed to fail.
The combat system relies on well timed parry moves and lethal stabs you can perform after a successful parry.
It takes a little time to get the hang of it, but once you understand the mechanic it will feel good.
Direct combat however is best avoided and the game is rather unforgiving, so don't expect to charge into a room, and kill 20 opponents with only a few strikes.
Combat is not the focus of this game, and it's all the better for it.
Platforming is also part of the experience.
As already mentioned before, Styx has to use the environment to his advantage.
This means that you can jump and climb on many things, hang on ledges, and use your platform gusto to get around the place.
The controls are very responsive, and if you connect a gamepad to your PC, the controls will soon be 2nd nature to you.
What I particularly liked was the fact that the climbing and jumping actually requires skill.
Styx can't just climb everywhere, and is not necessarily auto snapped to a surface. So getting around also requires you to use your brain and plan ahead. This feels strangely refreshing in a gaming landscape where platforming has become an easy access semi automatic thing.
So how is the game in term of graphics and sound design ?
Well in terms of graphics the game is above average and the art design is simply great.
Environments look beautiful and characters have a very unique feel to them.
The style can be described as comicy, yet things are still grounded in reality.
The world itself is largely medieval with a hint of steampunk.  Iseria is a well realized world with a lot of dark secrets, and the artstyle reflects this perfectly.
Technically the game runs smooth and it has some incredible lighting.
The charactermodels and textures could have benefited from some extra detail, yet the graphics do not disappoint.
The game's sound as stated before is great.
Especially the little details stand out, like the many different creaky noises a wooden floor can make.
Sound design is important in a stealth game, and Styx doen't disappoint.
Voiceacting is overall very good.
Some lines are delivered a little bland , and sometimes you will notice that certain bits of dialog are recycled, yet most of it is done very well.
For a game that was made under a very tight budget, it has some very nice production values, and it makes me wonder what this team is capable of when having a very high budget.
So this brings us to my conclusion.
Styx Master of Shadow is a very well made stealth RPG game that will bring you to a very different medieval fantasy world.
In terms of gameplay the game was made following the rules written in the "old school era".
That means that the game doesn't hold your hand, and is less accessible.
Ironically a game like this shows me the many things wrong with modern day game design.
While many modern games look amazing, they simply lack any bit of soul or substance.
This game made me truly feel like a shadow assassin. More than any Assassins Creed game ever did !
It might not be everyones cup of tea, but if you like a good challenge I would certainly recommend you to buy this game.

Ah man, where do I even start with IC. I suppose the first thing I should say is that I own a hard copy of the original game, bought during 2001 or so. I can't really remember why I wanted the game as I was just a kid; I guess I saw some really weird creatures on the front and thought "I want to play that game". Probably one of the best gut decisions I've ever made in regards to video games. I used to play this constantly as a kid, and even after growing up I'd still take a few hours here and there testing a new combination or playing a match. It wasn't until last year that I stopped due to my new computer not being able to play IC after an update. Fast forward to the end of the year and I, a new Steam user, happened to stumble upon this game once more.
Impossible Creatures is, as the Steam tags say, a RTS game through and through. However, it's a bit more complicated than that. As most of the game's page will point out, the units you control are all from your own design. Want a flying elephant? Just mix it with an owl. That not working out? Why not switch the elephant with a sperm whale? There 30-40+ animals for you to mix in match in this RTS to make the perfect 9 unit army. And if the base animal count isn't enough for you, there's plenty of mods out there for you to try and plenty of people to try these new creatures out on. Surprisingly, there's a lot of people still playing this game despite it being well over 10 years old, and thanks to Steam having a working online server, multiplayer battles are possible. Battles are pretty fluid, though perhaps a bit simple with more or less "throw your units in certain directions", but there's many ways to make a battle more interesting. If I were to summarize the game in general in 3 words, they'd be: simple, fun, and imaginative.
So I've been saying a lot of good about the game, but what's bad you might be asking. Well...not a lot, to be honest. The graphics are a bit dated (though they should be, this is an old game) but they don't look terribly bad. There's not much for solo play, but there is a single player mode and the base game has a short story mode which is nice. Also the units are a bit prone to lagging out (like they will take long pauses before doing something) if you have a lot of units in the world, but that's only in more extreme situations. Probably the biggest turn-off about the game is that not every unit is made equal; certain combinations are obviously better than others, but to an extent that makes sense. That isn't to say some unique combinations won't get you far and that tactics don't mean anything, but having certain combinations will definitely present you with an edge to the fight.
So what do I think about it? Certainly, it's a unique game in the RTS genre and certainly worth its price of $10. I recommend it to everyone. It's simple to pick-up and play, but you're really only limited in your ability to think up a creative way to solve a problem. And trust me there's many ways to solve problems here. This is a great game, and I (maybe foolishly) hope for the day I see Impossible Creatures 2 in development.
EDIT: Oh yeah, I also forgot. This game comes with a side component called "Mission Editor" (referred to as Impossible Creature Editor on Steam). What does this do? It allows you to make your own maps for your playing pleasure! And it's a surprisingly modern world editor for being 15+ years old. Everything molds smoothly (well, unless you literally make a pointed mountain), objects are well organized, various methods to edit the terrain aside from standard increase/decrease/smoothing tools...it's really good! The only thing I don't like about it is that you have to paint cliffs...no seriously, if you make a mountain, you need to put on mountain side textures to make it look different than the rest of the terrain (that said, I'm lazy so I don't want to do that).
So let's review; with this game, you get: a pretty good standalone RTS game with a unique feature (which is dated mind you, but still really good), a map editor for free for said game, free DLC automatically downloaded into the game, additional user-made "DLC" on Steam or online, online multiplayer...There's not much bad! And for $10 (and this edit was made when there was a sale, so that $10 is even lower!)! One note of caution though, this is a RTS game and thus suffers from standard RTS problems (some things are always better than othersfor example), but the unique "build-your-team" element more than makes up for that if you learn and understand how to counter certain units. That said, once again, this is a game well worth it's price.

If you’re looking for a quirky but fun adventure game to play then why not check out
, the story of a skeleton, friendship and plums? This game offers a unique story told through a point and click adventure game narrative with eye-catching artwork and hip music. If you enjoy classic adventure games from the 90’s and some laughs you should enjoy this game. I will say, however, the humor might not be to everyone’s fancy. While I found nothing in the dialogue offensive, it is clear not all of the jokes will hit their mark and some seem dated. That, however, does not deter from an all-around solid game.
The story centers around a teenage boy named Skinny, which is probably a nickname but this is never clarified. He’s hanging out with his friend, Ronald, and ends up eating a few plums, which he’s allergic to, and dies. No one knew about this allergy, and this comes as a schock, so much so his friend is traumatized to the point where he doesn’t speak anymore and blames himself. The whole goal of the game is for the now-skeletal Skinny to talk to his buddy Ronald and help him forgive himself, but that’s easier said than done since he waited too long to do it and is now on a time crunch. But Ronald’s family moves and most of the game involves Skinny tracking him down in the most convoluted way possible. At its heart, it’s a very sweet story but most of the things Skinny goes through are wacky and cartoonish. The writing is well done, it’s full of jokes and the quips of a main character with a sharp tongue. It’s full of cultural references, especially in the background but some jokes may not hit their mark for all players.
Since this is a point and click game, you mainly use your mouse to get through the story. You can click on an item and either look at it, pick it up, use it or talk to it and Skinny has lots of interesting dialogue depending on what you choose to do. People you can usually look at and talk to only, which makes sense. You also have an inventory system to hold items and you can also combine them there as well. Move around was fine, sure Skinny won’t run but he walks swiftly enough so transitioning airings didn’t seem sluggish. You also gain a map at a certain point in the game which allows you to teleport around town. The game also has puzzles to solve and this is where I became frustrated. Some of the solutions struck me as illogical. The game offers no guidance on what to do next, what items to use or combine, nothing. Some things made enough sense to figure it out without any help but honestly, I ended up using a guide to get through the game. Maybe I’m not very good at adventure games but it doesn’t seem intuitive to dip a red chili in green paint to make it a “jalapeno”, nor does it seem useful.
In the graphics department, the game does very well. Everything is very colorful and vibrant, despite the darker nature of the playing as a poor dead teen everything seems pretty happy. The characters are all unique and memorable, playing off well of the main character. The scenery is highly detailed and full of lots of Easter eggs and jokes. I was taken aback by the sheer number of hidden gems in the backgrounds and I’m certain I missed many of them. The game is fully voice acted and it’s done very well. I had no problem with any of the voice acting, even for the most minor of characters. There is also good music to accompany this package. Is it something I’d buy on a soundtrack? No -but it fit the game well and helped with the overall experience.
I enjoyed playing
but I didn’t enjoy needing to use a guide constantly. The game has Steam trading cards and achievements, but the achievements can also be very confusing. Without using a guide for them, you will probably miss at least half. Some are story related, others aren’t too hard to get by dumb luck or chance but some are just really out there. If you’re not concerned with achievements, however, this won’t be too much of an issue for you. Overall, is this the best adventure game? No. It’s fun and has a good story but I’d probably say grab it on sale if you’re looking to give it a try.

Styx: Master of Shadows is stealth game starring the eponymous protagonaist, Styx, an acerbic goblin in a world of men. Unlike most recent stealth games, Styx has ditched the trend for narrow, linear levels for large, mostly non-linear spaces with a huge amount of verticality.  Styx takes its gameplay and level design influences most from Dishonored and Thief 1 and 2.  Dishonored also seems to be the graphical style most emulated here; it's a pretty enough world, and I appreciated it's 'clean' style. It's clear that the developers looked to some of the best stealth games for inspiration.
Styx narrarates throughout the game, offering his cynical and often humorous take on the world around him.  Exploration and environmental storytelling help flesh out the story, which rarely resorts to lengthy exposition.  Voice acting is competent, though music was not memorable.
For those unfamiliar with the stealth genre, it's a type of game where the player is not the most powerful person in the world, unlike most action games. Unlike action games, also, when combat occurs it's because the player has messed up The player must avoid combat and hide, creating a wonderful tension.  The importance of hiding and finding a path around enemies connects the player to their environment in a way that most action and FPS game do not.
There is a great feeling of exploration and discovery in these levels, with multiple paths to take and secrets to discover.  Aiding Styx is a smart arsenal of items and powers that he can upgrade as the game progresses.  The AI is pretty standard, following set patrols and pursuing Styx if they spot him.  Beyond the basic guards are sprinkled a handful of other enemy types, including more powerful humans and some monsters.  It's refreshing to explore environments that don't treat the player like an idiot, and where every secret passage discovered feels like one that the player earned through experimentation and observation.
While level design is overwhelmingly the game's best quality, the same can not be said for combat. If a chasing enemy catches up to Styx, the game essentially becomes a frustrating QTE, which is bad enough.  However, other enemies are still active during this, and they will mercilessly attack Styx while he's helpless to run away.  I found these moments profoundly frustrating, since if you're caught in any of these moments and there's any more than one enemy around, you may as well sit back and go get a drink while the 15 second combat event plays out, since even if you do it flawlessly you'll be killed by an enemy against whom you cannot defend. I'm not sure what game the developers were looking to for inspiration here, but they should have simply emulated the model of Thief. A much simpler solution would have been to keep Styx, ditch the mini-game, and encourage him to simply run away.
The developers also seem to have taken the inspiration, rather poorly, from the original boss battles of Deus Ex for the game's 'final boss.' It's a clumsy, lasy, and, frustrating experience that left a sour taste in my mouth.  It's unfortunate that this was the last moment of the game, since nowhere else was this type of encounter attempted in the game.
Overall, despite these annoying flaws, Styx: Master of Shadows is a solid, enjoyable game that refreshingly treats the player like a patient adult and based its gameplay around building a world of interesting choices that reward observation and exploration.  It's a trend I'd like to see repeated.  I recommend this game to all fans of stealth titles.

It's an okayish game.
Pros:
It reminds me of the old Harry Potter games i used to play as a child. The secret locations and hideout seem to be inspired by those games.
Cons:
1. Extremely large amount of bugs, from random graphical glitches to being seen by the AI through walls. I have seriously been pulled through walls by the AI along with other serious gameplay bugs.
2. Gameplay is difficult for the sole purpose of being difficult. It's not challenging, just annoying as hell.
3. Linear gameplay. You are forced to play the exact way the developers want you to. An example of this is one of the earlier levels where you can't be seen or have a body seen otherwise you have to start over.
4. Extremely bad combat. More often than not it's literally impossible to fight people. It honestly makes Assassin's Creed's combat seem decent.
5. Lack of non-lethal gameplay. The only way you can deal with an enemy is by killing them loudly or quietly.
6. You're forced to search every inch of the map for random coins and if you don't get every single one, you don't get to have abilites that make the game less tedious.
7. There's a limit of around two of each item that you can carry. Want to have more than 2 of a disposable weapon or health potion? Too bad.
8. The darkness does not work at all. The enemies can easily see you which makes hiding in the dark quite useless. If you're hiding in the dark and just to happen to be in the 180 degree FOV of the AI, you're going to be instantly spotted and killed without warning.
9. Those roaby bugs. In an extremely tedious stealth game where you have to kill everyone, the developers thought it would be best to include a completely random creature in the game to annoy players even more. Regardless of the fact that they don't fit anywhere at all in the main story.
10.  The special vision. It's literally worse than any other magical vision in other games. It serves literally no purpose other than as an abitrary requirement to navigate through the poorly designed maps. Poor lighting with poor controls which need to be fixed with a "special ability" does not make a good game.
11. The clone. It also serves no purpose other than to solve trivial problems created by the developers for the sole reason of giving the clone a use in the game.
12. You can't look up or down. This isn't a joke, your body is blocking your view down and you can't move the camera up to see above you.
If you're looking for a decent stealth game instead, i suggest you try out Dishonored.

Sure, at first Hero Zero may just seem like your typical click and wait game. And it is very much a click and wait game, so if you absolutely hate those, don't expect much. However, and this is key, unlike other click and wait games it will never make you wait even half an hour for anything. In my opinion what makes those games so terrible is not that you have to click and wait, but that you have to click and then wait for so freaking long. The longest timers in HZ are about 20 mins, and those are pretty rare (there are also a couple 1 hour timers but those are for very special actions that you only need do once in a while anyways). Most don't go past 10 mins, and usually they are 5 mins or even less. In the meantime, there's plenty stuff to do so that you feel like you're always doing something even if it's just clicking and waiting. The game keeps you entertained, and isn't that what matters?
As for the pay to win issue, sure, of course if you spend real money you will get premium currency with which you will be able to level up faster (and come out stronger in the end). But again unlike other click and wait games, HZ doesn't make you feel like you're forced to buy premium or else the game becomes practically unplayable. You won't have the most pimped out, overpowered character, but there are plenty players who don't buy premium and you're always competing and progressing steadily along with them. The game is funny and even pleasant, so you might even like it enough to support it and get some basic packages that will make it that much more smoother and enjoyable. But hey, the best part is you don't have to take my word for it, because it is completely free to try out and in my opinion very much worth doing so!

So far I don't have much time in the game and have only done a little exploring and playing with various blocks and tools to see what is available. My impressions so far are extremely positive. I was previously playing another voxel based building game called Landmark which while full of potential ultimately failed due to a lack of direction and numerous game-breaking voxel bugs. Not to mention over complexity when it comes to making small details and corporate politics. Microvoxel warping was annoying as hell. However in Rising World we have planks and poles, which can be resized and precisely rotated to build up any shape you wish for without distorting the surrounding blocks. There's even the option to use PNG images as decals for the purpose of wall art, rugs and assorted details that may prove too small to model. One Night Stand is a short and sweet choose your own adventure type of game/highly interactive VN. It takes a familiar scenario and delivers the most entertaining morning after you've ever had.
Soundtrack
The soundtrack was carried mostly by sweet little guitar riffs that were a little too subtle for my liking. It gives a feeling of mystery but goes completely missing during dialoge. I have to add that it actually made the intentional awkwardness feel more authentic this way but some sort of alternative riff for those parts would have helped elevate the dialoge.
Gameplay
As with any VN you do a lot of reading in this game. The difference is that you have the opportunity to investigate your surroundings to use for conversation later which in turn changes up the dialoge. This gives you some surprisingly varied play throughs. I found it to be a much better approach than the traditional conversation pathing you normally see in a VN. Rather than each choice leading to an absolute path hidden behind multiples of text you've already experienced. You can dig up alternative dialogue which usually indicates you're onto a different ending but still end up in one you've already experienced. This led to me not useing the skip button as often as I would in most other VN's that I have played.
Story
This game doesn't have much of a story. It just presents you with a scenario. One that plays out with a lot of humanity and takes the story to more realistic territory. In addition, there is a mysterious girl's bedroom for players to explore in order to learn more about her. The kicker is that the game only feeds you bits of the person she could be. Suggesting a lot but ultimately leaving the decision up to the player. Very effective stuff.
Graphics
The art style of the game is charming. It's not the most cutting-edge but it just reinforces that authenticity in the game. I was expecting the character to be just still images that transition from one another but the way it is done here, although essentially the same has been presented in such a way that it distances itself from the traditional approach VN's normal take. There is a mix of actual animation between the image still transitions and that helps breath life into it. The washed out water color look suites the game. The only complaint is that the indicator in the main menu that is supposed to show which option is highlighted contrasts with the background way too much and makes it difficult to tell what option you are selecting.
This game is very down to earth and light hearted with some great endings and interesting dialgue and presentation. The price for the game is more than fair and honestly for what you get it's great value. I whole heartedly enjoyed the game and would recommend this to anyone even slightly interested in VN's. I think it's done better than most even if the story may not be as robust. If you're interested by the game in any way, I'd say that's more than enough justification here to buy it and again for such a cheap price it's hard to see anyone walking away dissapointed.

Disclaimer: This is a summarized review for a later more complex review. I have not completed my first playthrough yet, but I am very near the end.
Valdis Story is a game that I am currently super conflicted on. It is an amazing action game with pretty good RPG elements, stacked on top of a mediocre at best Metroidvania and a simple, but respectable story.
Good:
-4 different playable characters, each with up to 4 unique weapons they can use with different movesets
-Very intuitive 2D combat. Those who are skilled in chaining combos will find this game to have an incredible amount of depth and flow to how combat works. Magic and attacks weave incredibly well, and there is a plethora of intriguing extra features that add to the combat, giving you a massive depth of options at any single moment.
-Enjoyable art style. Overall, I really enjoy the art in this game, and think that it looks really good in motion. The animation as well is fluid and easy to read.
-Interesting story. It isn't high end super grade narrative, but it is also not trying to be. It tells its story and it makes it feel interesting. The main character in general was really enjoyable to see as you learn his origins and his viewpoints in the war he is in.
Cons:
-My biggest gripe overall is that this game almost constantly expects the player to backtrack. Now I understand that this is a common theme in Metroidvania games, but this game makes it less than enjoyable as the back tracking isn't always for things of value. Random useless materials, There is no way to fast travel back to a town, so digging deeper into the world just to get essentially nothing and having to walk all the way back is an absolute chore and drain on the enjoyment.
-Following up on the first point, the lack of valuable items in the world is clearly a forced scenario. There is a material in the game that you only get 10 of per run, and all 10 are required to make the final weapon for each character. These materials can also be used to upgrade other items in the game. AT NO POINT DO THEY TELL YOU THIS! You can completely miss a weapon in the game simply because there is never some sort of warning that the material itself is limited.
-Following up on that, this is a common issue that can happen multiple times. As of current, there is a village that if you do not complete a quest that is mostly mentioned in passing, then that village will essentially be destroyed. You will lose all the vendors and characters inside of that place if you don't do this quest, and there is no warning or guidance on how to do it. It simply exists, and you have to figure it out before progressing too far.
-THERE IS NO TRUE NEW GAME PLUS. This is a massively stupid decision in my opinion. There is so many collectibles in the game, and there is no purpose in getting basically any of them because you will lose virtually everything when you start a new run through. The only things you will keep are weapons, which being some of the weapons you get so late in the game, and one can be missed entirely, I question them even locking weapons behind progress in the first place. There is currently no way around this, so when you play through, do not have a completionist attitude, it won't help you at all.
-Double jump is unlocked through an NPC you find and send back to your home base, and requires materials to get. Everything else in the game you get just by playing it, but double jump is the only one that you have to purchase. Some areas seem like you need double jump to do basically anything, and this NPC can be entirely missed. Just poor design.
Overall, I want to say that it is a good game. It is 2 years old, so every gripe I have may be a norm from back then. I still love this game, because the combat is incredibly fun and really never gets stale. I hate the poor effort on the metroidvania elements, but honestly, the game feels so much fun to play that I don't have much an issue with them.
I recommend playing this game, but please know that if you want to play this game, do not set expectations high for the metroidvania elements. Combat is where this game shines
