Castlestorm is a semi-automatic tower defense game with elements from MOBAs and strategy games set in medieval fantasy world. You take control over one army and battle another one in a 2D Environment, Sending troops to do battle and supporting them with a full control siege crossbow.
I had this game laying around for over a year I think before I started playing it. I regret not picking it up earlier. The main reason that drew me towards it, was it's graphic design. It has a colorful cartoony art style that reminds me of a more recent version of the Warcraft 3 engine while the gameplay feels a little like Orks must Die.
After playing it first, it did not expect to like it. I usually don't dig tower defense games, as they bore me rather quickly. This one, I enjoyed however. The combat feels slick, theres lots of variety in both siege ammunition and troops and together with the DLC the campaigns are fairly long. When I stopped this game, it left me with a desire to want more. I was motivated to take on the campaign levels once again to get better ratings!
Of course, this game is not perfect. You could argue theres too much focus on the crossbow combat, the multiplayer on the internet is practically non existent as of the date of writing of this review, the single player highscores are bloated with hackers and impossible to reach scores, the hero combat is a little simplistic and the castle builder mode is fairly hard to use.
But if you overlook this, you get a decent game thats a load of fun and I have to say it has by far the best vikings I've seen in over 10 years. Blew my mind. Also, the music was made by the artist Waterflame, who produced a big deal of tracks for Castle Crashers.
I hereby recommend this game for a purchase. Pick it up when it's on sale. Or just now if you like.

It's hard to complain about repetitive, recolored enemies and relatively simple attack combos in a brawler. For better or worse, those are staples of the genre. By those standards, Phantom Breaker: Battlegrounds actually does pretty well. There's decent enemy variety, especially as you reach later stages, and as you progress you can unlock longer and more varied combos.
But therein lies the problem. Unlock. This is one of those games in which you have a progression system, it's quite slow and grindy, and you're forced to choose between boring but powerful statistical upgrades and the special abilities that actually make the combat fun. I was able to get to a point where I both had enough damage that enemies didn't take an annoyingly long time to kill, and could deal that damage in interesting ways – but in exchange I had to completely ignore defense. To raise both to the levels I would expect in a brawler, I'd have had to double my play time on the earlier stages. Since I was already getting bored with the game by the time it started to become fun, I didn't have much incentive to press on.
Did I mention that those unlocks were for one character, and the game has several, each with their own abilities and dialogue?
Once you finally have enough unlocked that it feels like a complete game, Phantom Breaker: Battlegrounds is a solid brawler. The sprites are large, detailed and cute, the enemies have interesting attack patterns, and locking your character and your opponents onto "tracks" in the foreground and background proves a clever way to smooth out the positional ambiguity that occasionally haunts the genre. It just can't make up for how long it takes before the game gets fun.

Only buy this game when it is on sale. It is not worth $10. The $5 I bought it for is about right. This game could have been great, but instead is merely mediocre, and all because of the poor unit mechanics.
The storyline is fun and engaging, but any actual control over your hero is close to imaginary.
The response time to shield against attacks is laughable, you can only see 3 feet in front of you, and you give up control over your best weapon (the ballista)
Ground based unit fights are done in an unusual style. each unit stops to fight only one other letting all other enemis past.
For example, if you have 2 soldiers against 1 enemy one of your soldiers and theirs will engage and your second will walk right past.
This might not seem like much until you get larger units with splash attacks. Trolls and the like can kill several of your units will one hit but only one of yours even gets to attack.
This combat is even more poorly implemented when you add in the ballista and flying units. The ballista shots damage your own units, and it can easily become impossible to fire without hitting your own units
The flying combat is even more disjointed and tacked on. I have never had a single ranged ground unit take out a flyer. You have to shoot them down yourself.
Coupled with said flyers ducking and bobbing randomly, as well as dealing splash damage attacks (and one hit killing most units), this is a huge oversight and in many cases ruins and otherwise fun game time.
The organization of the game is foolishly repetative. In both kingdom/royal guard, and Viking/viking elites factions the units are almost interchangeable, but upgrades must be bought separately.
Separate upgrades must be bought for all of the support buildings as well, even though these are exactly the same across all classes. This is true of some of the Heros/Heroins too.

A great entry into a thin genre, Styx is a fun and challenging stealth focused game. The game does not have any real combat mechanics resulting in a Parry/Kill system when you are caught by guards. Getting seen and not escaping before the guard reaches you creates a 1v1 fight where Styx can dodge or parry attacks. Only after a few parries can you dispatch your foe. The game offers an "open world" feel by allowing you multiple pathways to achieve your goals.  There have been several times I cleared a room only to look around and see an easier path I could have taken. The game offers a bare bones upgrade system that give you a reason to explore each area as you look for "Insignia". These gold coins are strewn across each area and most can be located without too much searching.  The situations the game presents to the player seem to be well balanced and do require some thought without making you feel cheated. The real negative (and this is a big negative) is Styx's ability to traverse the enviroment. Invisible edges, ungrabbable ledges, iffy platforming all combine to cause more deaths then any enemy. Some extra attention by the developer could have smoothed these platforming issues and would have resulted is a lot less fustration. All in all I do recommend Styx: Master of Shadows to anyone that enjoys a stealth focused action game just be ready to miss a few jumps and fall to your death.

This game is similar to MtG, and perhaps the most well-designed game of its kind, but sometimes suffers from its relatively low budget.
In MTG vs hearthstone, there are three major design differences: mana, combat, and instants. Spellweaver gets all of those points right:
1) Just like in MtG, lands are used to produce mana and you can have cards from multiple classes, but there is a lot more deck control in Spellweaver, so you very rarely run out of lands to place.
2) In Hearthstone the attacker would always choose who he attacks, and in Magic the defender would always decide. In Spellweaver, they have a speed stat for each creature, and higher speed creatures can block lower speed creatures; if they are not blocked they can attack whatever they want. It's a nice compromise that also adds some room for card diversity.
3) Instants exist in Spellweaver (and so add more depth to the game), but they don't slow the game down because they can only be played at certain times. So you get most of the depth of instants without having to pass priority after every card.
The game suffers a little from its low budget (the kickstarter only got $10k when the final goal was $15k, and it's made by a 5-man dev team that took 4 years to release it):
1) It's not too pretty. The card art is mediocre, worse than MtG or hearthstone imo. There are very few animations, i.e. if someone plays a card that says they instantly win you will only see the win screen, not how they won. The sounds are also fairly repetitive and lackluster.
2) You can't chat in-game. You can add friends and then chat after, but still.
3) The game has a pretty small playerbase, so they might stop developing it at some point... :/

What Remains of Edith Finch presents itself as the story of a girl discovering how the last five generations of her family died. At first, the stories seem disjointed, but subsequent playthroughs reveal a clever continuity between each death and the true story of the Finch family. While the true cause of many of the deaths is obscured, players are given the details to find out what really happened themselves. The result is that the first two-hour playthrough merely gives players the pieces to the puzzle, but it takes another playthrough or two to piece them together. Altogether, What Remains of Edith Finch is a wonderful game with a deceptively large amount of content for what is a two-hour game at first glance.

I am a huge fan of stealth games. I love them. It's like a puzzle in and of itself trying to figure out how to use the environment and resources available to you in order to make it around enemies without detection. The combat in this game is not meant to be good combat. You're a small goblin whose specialty is hurling daggers, picking locks, and sneaking around. He is by no means a fighter and can only do so much, so anyone expecting a combat-oriented game is going to be in for a very rude awakening.
My major complaint however is the repetitiveness of the NPCs when they spot you. Every single time it's always, "A monster!" and "This one's mine!" There is extremely little variation and to be honest makes every screwup a grating exercise just because I want to avoid hearing those lines spoken. All the men in the game sound the same and spoken lines sound forced and emotionless and even downright silly in some cases.
However overall I give this a recommendation to those who like these kinds of old-school stealth games. Don't expect it to be easy and don't expect much in the way of hand-holding. There's little fluff to it. You're given a goal or two in a mission and it's up to you to work out the puzzle from start to finish in the way you feel is best.

It took me a bit to get into Spellweaver but after I got the hang of the new TCG systems I was hooked. I like the idea of being able to shift creatures around and to break through the enemy lines with speed. Spellweaver takes the idea of strategy in a TCG and turns it up to 11 with having to manage speed, front line and support line, and order level. All of these new concepts combine to make each turn an opportunity to turn the tide of a match. Spellweaver is designed for the players who enjoy the strategic depth of classic MTG and the freedom of deckbuilding.
Pros:
Charming Presentation
Tons of Strategy
Robust deckbuilding
Really good tutorial
Fair pay model
New concepts like speed, positioning, and order levels
Cons:
Limited player base
Balance issues
Small card pool
Spellweaver marries the depth and strategy of MTG to the charm and simplistic nature of Hearthstone to create a fun and unique take on the digital TCG genre.

Good:
+ Environment art.
+ Interesting lore.
+ Beautiful music.
+ Simple but effective skill trees.
+ Sometimes the fun outshines the annoyance.
+ Seems fairly bug-free.
Bad:
- Wonky movement, sometimes made worse by icy areas that make your character slide. More universally, jumping doesn't seem very "precise," which is consistently annoying. I don't know if detection boxes are aligned strangely relative to the artwork or what, but this was a complaint of mine when I first got into the game a year or two back. It hasn't changed.
- Only two characters, with two others locked until you finish the game. All of them are pasty anime kids (with possible exception to the locked half-dragon lady). In three hours of gameplay, the only customization I've noticed is in some hard-to-find gear that isn't reflected visually on the characters, and the skill trees.
- Irritating boss fights that don't get any better on Normal.
- The story (up to the point I've reached) isn't very strong, and the dialogue fails to pick up the slack with character development. This all adds up to me having no incentive to slog onward.
I've tried "Valdis Story: Abyssal City" twice, with a long break in between, and there's just something off about the mechanics. Perhaps my lack of passion for hardcore platforming is part of the problem here, but I've nonetheless thoroughly enjoyed some other side-scrolling titles with much less going for them ("Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams" comes to mind, which I expected to hate but wound up loving).
Not worth $14.99. Arguably not worth $4.99. Definitely not worth any more of my time.

Aside from this I am genuinely pretty happy about the game. The art, the way the story is told, the music. They all come together beautifully in a way that has me wanting more. Introduction
Due to my fascination of World War II era tanks I soon found on the internet a PC game which I thought would meet my taste for tank conquest.  Men of War: Assault Squad is a strategy/tactical game that takes place during World War II. The user is allowed to play just about nearly every faction, with each having its own uniqueness.
Pros/Cons
I first bought this game in the middle of July, with the purpose of finding a game more sided towards tank warfare. Having already logged 40 hours since purchasing, I consider myself an avid intermediate user. An Ideal user of this game would be someone who is fascinated with PC gaming and can handle a couple hours of sitting. While I wouldn’t recommend using the most basic computer available I did find it was supportive on most basic systems that are relatively new. My 3.5 star rating was comprised of three things:
•	Difficulty
•	Faction Uniqueness
•	Tank Integration
Difficulty – This game is very difficult to the new user. Perhaps almost too difficult if not on the right setting. It took me a couple hours just to get the mechanics of the game and how to play it effectively. Ultimately, though this is a challenge and as a dedicated gamer I can never say no to a challenge.
Faction Uniqueness – This aspect of the game left me with my mouth open. Unlike most other games, every unit faction is somehow representative of its country in terms of performance and equipment. Especially with tanks I found this the greatest, as no two tanks were ever the same.
Tank Integration – I was actually a bit saddened by this part. I initially was looking for a game that was more individualized to tank play. While tank play in this game is one of the most important keys, I found it to be a bit limiting with their use as the tanks are just one aspect of an army. Compounded with the micro control of every unit and the tanks seem a bit down played.
Conclusion
Overall I was pretty happy about my purchase of the game. Being a college student, I can’t afford a nice graphics card at this time, and found this game was able to meet my demands for gameplay and entertainment. I would recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a challenging strategy war game.

First of all, this is not a game engine like Unity or GameMaker.
Construct 2 is just an HTML5 game IDE. That means your resulting game is limited to what can be done in HTML5.
If you plan on making a really simple 2D platform game, or a simple puzzle game, this is for you.
If you have some unique mechanics in mind, you better go with Unity.
Construct 2 is great until you need to do something that isn't provided.
In that case you have to learn some Javascript, look under the hood, and make your own "behavior" (that's a name for construct2 element definitions).
Also, as some other people said, get the Scirra version.
tl;dr get it for simple simple typical games, don't get it for original games

Hearthstone and Magic the Gathering had a baby.. A really awesome baby.
The mechanics are similar to both titles and the card art is gorgeous. The free to play model is fair I find and I'll go into detail on that shortly.
As you play matches you earn gold (Free Earnable Currency) and fame (XP) You can play against AI or against other people and have the option of playing Friendly matches or Ranked games that give you a rating. All cards can be earned through just playing the game and it doesnt feel like your being drip fed a miniscule amount of currency to reach that goal of obtaining more cards and decks.
The deck Building is similar to Magic the Gathering in that you have multiple colours to choose from each with their own gimmicks and playstyles, You can mix them up how you see fit and create a customised deck suited to your playstyle.
Upon first entering the game you are given a choice of 1 of the 6 starter decks available (Which are still somewhat competitive against real people even without adding in cards earned through quests or buying with real money I might add)
Upon reaching level 5 (Roughly a couple hours of gameplay for me) You are given another starter deck and this is were the fun begins.. You can mix your two starter decks together to create a duo element deck as I touched on earlier.
For instance my Order deck (White token and flying focused for those that play MTG) and my newly acquired Nature deck (Elven Aggro which consists of low cost fast creatures and instant speed spells) were mixed together to create a deck that has more options instead of sticking to a set one trick pony strategy and allowing for more variation in what you can do in your player matches.
As you level up you will acquire Rewards for doing so, such as Gold and Packs you could otherwise purchase on the store.
Normal Packs contain 10 random cards and there are also good and evil Booster packs if your looking to get something from those specific factions. Good = Order,Nature and Wisdom/  Evil = Rage, Corruption and Dominion.
There is also a draft format with tournaments being held for prizes and these are unlocked later as you level.
Ranked matches are unlocked at level 3 giving you time to be eased into the game and learn its mechanics.
All in all I really recommend this game, It's free, Fun and you don't have to spend a penny to have a good time although if you want to support the devs I recommend purchasing a double box for either good or evil depending on the factions you want to play with.

Do you want to play a fighting game that's more about out thinking than out combo-ing? Do you ever wish that you could just trick your opponent to win, rather than killing them? Did you play Bushido Blade, and miss throwing your sword? This is the game you are looking for.
Nidhogg is a two player fighting game where the faster reflexes don't always beat the more calculated approaches. A constant battle of wits versus reflexes, where every move has a counter move, and prediction is just as valid as reaction. What it lacks in depth of mechanics (this game would have been at home on the original NES with its two button plus joystick controls) it makes up for in its easily accessed depth of play. People who are new to fighting games are still able to compete with more veteran players, making this an ideal game for casual multiplayer bouts.
While it has a single player mode, this game is designed for two or more people to share, ideally with a group, in a big cozy livingroom.

This game I guess you could say is a "metroidvania" platformer, but more spefically the feel, level themes, and music really remind me of Castlevania: Symphony of The Night. However, the fighting style is a lot more involved in this game and allows you to use a variety of different spells (you can equip four a a time). The controls are mostly smooth and allow for quicker combat than you usually have in these types of games (although I occasionally had a hardtime parrying attacks).
My one main complaint about the game is that the story seems to left a lot unexplained, like, a couple more sentences at the beginning of the game would have made more sentence. It's not to say they left it all together, there's a lot of talk about gods and goddess, angels and demons and our angry hero who hates all of them, but you never really get a sense of who the characters actually are, which makes me wonder why the even bothered with the dialogue. I would also say that the bosses at the end of the game are quite a bit harder than ones you'll fight previously...if you make to the end of the game prepare for a couple of very frustrating fights. Additionally, a global map would have been very helpful, not ones that were partitioned with the three seperate stations. In a game like Castlevania where you have to revisit things and travel long distances, it always helps to keep track of where those things are- it was a little difficult in this game.
Despite my complaints, I still enjoyed the game overall and would recommend to anyone who enjoyed Symphony of the night or enjoys atmospheric "metroidvania" style games.

It might look like hot garbage, or art, depending on where you fall in terms of visual preference. It might be stupidly simple, or elegantly uncomplex, depending on how you feel about the gameplay. It might be the greatest fighting game ever made, or an overpriced hipster art project, depending on if you like the damn thing or not. In development since 2011, this side-scrolling two-player fighting game where you duel with swords, kicks, runs, jumps and fistfights has been turning heads. Either towards it, attracted to the bright Atari-style low-fi graphics and immediately comprehensible combat, or away from it in disgust because… reasons.
It’s an incredible fast paced game when both players (or the player vs A.I.) are reckless. Pixel blood flows down the walls as each fighter tries to get past the other. If you make it, you move to the next screen and your opponent is placed in front of you once more. It’s a tug of war, in a sense. The victor not decided by who kills who the most, but by whichever side reaches their goal first: a giant flying worm on either end of the level. If you can get eaten by the Nidhogg, you have proven your prowess in combat.
But it can also be a slow, methodical and beautiful game of lethal Chess.

King's Bounty is above all else a strategy game with role playing elements tossed in. However, it gets the mix of the genres right which turns in to long and arduous; but fun, battles and exploration. The game runs on Normal skill at roughly 50-60 hours long and much longer on any higher difficulty but I highly recommend Normal for a challenge. The locales are varied, there is almost no VO but the story is intriguing (what little there is). The gameplay is solid and the characters interesting enough. Battles are balanced as are the skill trees of the 3 classes (Warrior, Mage, Paladin) as well as their weaknesses being balanced in combat. I highly recommend this game to anyone who loves Strategy based games with a lot of time on their hands.. and patience.

Now here's an overlooked gem.
Men of War: Assault Squad is not your typical RTS Starcraft-wannabe game, no fast paced tactics and throwing mobs at the enemy, unless you happen to really, REALLY hate the guys you're commanding or you're reenacting Russian penal battalions. Assault Squad requires you to carefully look at the battlefield and plan your attacks. Even then you will fail, all because you didn't notice that one AT gun or one MG gunner inside that house. The battles are brutal and often over before you can even blink thanks to the other guy getting off a lucky shot on that shiny, expensive, oh-so-fabulous Tiger tank you just called in that you planned your whole push around.
This game is very much detail oriented and microing, right down to making sure your soldiers and vehicles have enough ammo. If they don't, get ready for some manual resupply or battlefield scavenging. Don't be surprised if you're playing as the Americans and you have squads completely equipped with German weapons because that was what was on hand. Speaking of taking enemy weapons, disabled enemy vehicles and abandoned/you-slaughtered-the-crew-with-no-mercy AT gun positions can be repaired and used by your own guys. No bigger "♥♥♥♥ you" than blowing up an enemy position with their own fancy equipment.
All in all, I wholeheartedly recommend MoW: AS, it's a much different take on the RTS genre, and a refreshing one at that. The only real downside to the game is a lack of maps for singleplayer, but the ones that are there are very nice with a good amount of replayability, which helps mitigate this somewhat.
It took me way too long to figure out what was going on, but now that I can do I frankly can't get enough of this game. For Strategy/RPG buffs who don't mind a little leg work in their grinding.

A true sequel in my opinion should always strive to be better than it's predecessor, while at the same time keeping true to the essence of what made the original great.  Memoria does this, with it's improved performance, smoother animations, larger scope and vision of narrative, and willingness to try new things. As in my review of the prequel, "Chains of Satinav", I would almost say that I recommend playing this game simply if you are a fan of finely crafted Fantasy-  regardless of liking for point-and-clicks.  Geron the Bird Catcher's tale continues in this stunningly executed chapter in the Dark Eye universe, and it is here we are also introduced to the mysterious bits and pieces of a story set in the long forgotten past...  of a young woman seeking to overcome Time itself, and an ensorcelled staff willing to help her achieve this goal.  In summary:
Pros:
+ Fun and creative puzzle solving mechanics in place that require you to consider all aspects of an environment, and think outside the box
+ Top notch voice acting-  perhaps even improved from before. Fitting to each of the characters, with a wide variety and personality for even background/minor individuals
+ Fantastic digital painting style of art
+ The soundtrack! Adventurous and moving in it's execution, which sets a different tone for the setting of the narrative vs. the prequel. Play both to see what I mean
+ Conclusion felt completely satisfying, yet still left me ready for more, should Daedalic offer it
+ Sadja as a secondary protagonist felt well developed as a character...  and her companion the Staff was just great to listen to. The relationship they develop is a fascinating one, and the more I discovered about his origins, the more I felt myself caring about the fate of both him and his Princess
+ Limited dialogue choices included to immerse the player in the scenario
Neutrals/Cons:
- Lip synching was still kind of off in places, and left something to be desired
- A "certain character's" actions at a "certain point" seemed somewhat out of the blue, but may have been allowed to take place in order to highlight the corrupting influence of selfish want and desire
- A guide or at least a few hints may be required at some point to proceed. Just as solving a tricky puzzle can make you feel good about yourself, clicking that hint button one or a dozen times, only to see something so obvious that you missed out of impatience/lack of observation can make you feel really dumb haha
Overall:
9 out of 10
Memoria is a wonderful, quality adventure game with a storyline that kept me enthralled throughout.  I enjoyed playing as Sadja, and though the dynamic set in motion between the first game's protags was indeed touching, I kind of wished we had gotten to directly engage a bit more with her painful history in the same capacity as Geron's, with perhaps just a bit more epilogue. That's really just nit-picking though. Seriously, check out both this AND Chains of Satinav-  a pair of gems just waiting to be picked up.

Memoria is a sequel to Chains of Satinav.  In my opinion, I would highly recommend playing CoS first.  While most of the story in Memoria is new, it is framed by the story/characters coming from CoS.  In the least, you will feel more invested in those characters while playing Memoria, which enhances the experience.
I don't discuss plots in reviews much, but will say that Memoria is two stories in one. The first being a continuation of CoS that frames the story within the story.  The second story is a tale of a young princess who lived 400 or so years in the past.
The dual story device here is both a blesssing and a burden in an otherwise very good game.  You get to continue to play with characters from CoS that you care about and are invested in, while learning their fates.   Yet, that part of the story feels a bit short and unsatisfying as probably most fans of the first game would like.  The other tale though is very good with some very solid adventure type gameplay.
Again, following from my CoS review, the art style, voice acting and music are all excellent.  The art style here seems a bit more refined/modern than the more painted feel of CoS, but is no less great.  I found the puzzles in the game to be generally harder than CoS, with a good many being quite unintuitive.  There are some real stretches here.  I have to admit that my lack of patience caused me to peak in at a walkthrough at least 2 or 3 times to get moving.  But overall still very enjoyable.
The story and adventures of Sadja - in the inner tale from the past - is really very nice and satifying from begining to end.   The framing tale of Geron and Nuri, while solid, felt a bit less so, but it is still very good and marries nicely with the other tale.  If you've played CoS I think you will understand what I mean, but just don't want to comment on that directly in the review so as not to impact the objectively of a new player experiencing the game.
A very solid companion piece to Chains of Satinav,  with the combined two games providing plenty of hours of strong adventure type gameplay and story telling.  Certianly a must for fans of the genre.  I hope we one day see more games to continue the main characters stories.

A short but decent graphic adventure which reminded me a lot of the old adventure games from the 90s. I beat the game in roughly 9 hours (with pauses due to real life where the game was left running).  If you marathoned it without getting up and are good at puzzles, you could finish it much faster.
The ending was probably the least interesting part of the adventure since your final choices are much more limited than I would have preferred.  Unlike some people, I did not encounter any crashes or stability issues.  The only problem was occassional lag in certain cutscenes and animations (which I am shocked about considering its a mostly 2D game and my computer is a monster).  Anyways, my overall verdict would be to purchase it on sale if you want to experience a more old-school style adventure game with pretty background visuals, just don't expect the story to blow your mind.

Spellweaver is, in my opinion, the best CCG out right now. I haven't had so much fun creating decks and challening players since the early years of Magic The Gathering. I currently have 8 pages worth of decks based around different ideas and synergies and it is only going to increase with the expansions!
The Artwork is amazing and really pulls you in. The mechanics are innovative yet familiar, drawing the best features from games like Hearthstone and MTG yet improving upon them and making them distinct and original.
There are top players from MMDoC and M:TG who play this game and it is great getting to see them on the leaderboards.
The quest and rewards system is VERY generous for a FTP, if you are an average player you can expect to build some very competitive decks within a few days of simple questing. If you are very skilled you can play Trials and probably get a full set in 3 months. Compare that to Hearthstone where it could take you over a year! While an amazing FTP game, I encourage everyone to take advantage of the 40% bonus crystals for the Steam release.
But perhaps the best part of this game is the Dev team; a small group of independant developers that really listen to the community and seem to constantly be working on and improving elements of the game based on player feedback. Their creativity is novel and exciting; just when you think a card is going to be fixed or nerfed in a predictable way, they surprise you with their innovative thinking.
Believe me, after playing Spellweaver with it's Divine Offering mechanic, skill shrine abilities, hero powers and creature Speed mechanic, it is very difficult to go back to playing other CCGs. They have done the seeming impossible by minimizing RNG while maximizing deck variance. Definitely recommend playing this game if you are even slightly interested in CCGs (and even if you are not!)

The people who designed this game have absolutely 0% grasp of good game design, they actually managed to mash together the WORST features from several different card games and tries passing it off as enjoyable, when it's anything but.
Not only does it have the attrocious game mechanic where your summoned minions can attack other summoned minions directly, which just leads to horribly steamrolly games where a slight edge at any point in the game turns into way disproportionate board leads, they even had the bad taste to make damage heal after each turning, meaning that a player on the back foot doesn't even have the option of killing the winning players winning minion in a "death through a thousand cuts style", which would have at least been a slight upside. The game doesn't even contain anything that resembles decent removal cards, which I guess in their twisted logic is to compensate for the fact how effective removal the minions can be, but all this means is there are even fewer venues for comeback for a player on the back foot.
Furthermore, they even adopted Magic's style of having your scaling resource to play cards with be part of the deck itself, which means that you can fail to draw said resource. This kind of mechanic is fine for a paper card game as it is subject to physical limitations, but there is absolutely no excuse for a stand-alone digital card game working this way. None. Zip. Zero. This said, I realize they implemented an in-game mechanic to have a chance to draw extra "shrines" as they're called, but the fact that they felt compelled to add this arbitrary button to the game speaks volumes of how much of a bad idea the mechanic is.
Oh, and as an alternative to actually taking the time to design a decent AI they just give the "PvE" encounters that are supposed to be challenging ridiculous bonuses like starting with extra resources or cards, which like every time this kind of thing is pulled just amounts to playing something other than the actual game itself. It doesn't teach me or help the player in any way or form to transition into playing against real players and is honestly just always lazy game design.
Add to this that cards, and whole factions, are poorly balanced between each other and just a very poorly designed user interface in general leaves very little to nothing to make this game worth considering.
My advice is to stay away. Spend your time doing literally anything else.

This is a collectible, tactical and strategic, fantasy card game; a worthy successor to Magic: The Gathering ( M:TG ). This is a high quality game, in the same vein as "Spectromancer" ( free on Kongregate ) and "Infinity Wars".
"Spellweaver" features 4 different speed types for creatures ( think of a slow, lumbering giant or hydra that does massive damage, versus a swift elf that does lower damage - kind of like David versus Goliath ).
A lot of thought was put into overcoming mana problems. Lands ( shrines ) create both coloured and colourless mana, which become fixed, depending on your choice ( depending on the cards in your hand ). You also have the option to dump a card from your hand, draw 5 cards at random from your deck, and pick one land ( shrine ) if any - a mechanic that takes advantage of modern computing power.
Pros:
- Once you get over the learning curve of the game's speed mechanics, and timing of spells, the game becomes very absorbing.
- I love the artwork and the music is nice. My favourite card art:
- The developers are very generous. You get a free booster deck every 5 levels, starting with level zero. By the time I was level 10, I had three different decks and made a couple of interesting dual-colour, combo decks. You can go on quests and gain gold and booster packs. Tips for beginners: buying "Normal" packs of 10 random cards for 12,500 gold is the best value for in-game money. In the beginning you might focus on good or evil packs but those cost 17,500 gold for 10 cards.
- You can practice against AI of different difficulties and they are somewhat Godly on Expert or Inhumane difficulty.
- I found a game at any time of day, even at 4:30 am ( North American Eastern time ) 1 minute queue time rather than 20 seconds, during peak time. If you don't want to wait, there is always AI.
- Gets very addictive around level 5. I've been playing for 36+ hours straight. I passed out at my keyboard, min-maxing and re-designing my decks. I had just finished an "Epic Quest" ( 55 PVP battles ) and won a 12-pack box ( 12 x Normal Packs = 120 cards total ). Then I stumbled to the washroom before my pants filled up:
- I recently noticed that there is crafting ( to craft missing cards ) trials ( drafting ) and public tournaments. I just finished my first Trial ( a draft game against other human opponents ). The competition is top notch in Trials, which is fantastic. Two entry tickets were given to me for free by the developers, so based on my final performance ( 2 losses, 1 win and a final loss ) I ended up winning 2 x small packs + 1,000 gold.
Cons:
- The game mechanics regarding speed are confusing at first, so there is a bit of a learning curve, via trial and error.
- The card sets are currently tiny: around 31 different cards per colour. More cards are coming out in a few months.
- After playing for 36-48 hours straight, I got bored of seeing the same colours utilizing the same mechanics. I wish that there was a format for larger, pre-constructed decks ( I like to use 80- 100 dual-colour card decks. 100 card libraries are the maximum size and 60 cards are the minimum deck size ). Streamlined, 60 card decks are fun to make but they eventually get boring to play with or against. When I played Magic: The Gathering, my friends and I would use 2,000 card, rainbow libraries.
- The server is occasionally, annoyingly flaky giving you a, "You were disconnected from the server" errors ( usually a problem while trying to login to the game but a couple of times, I've been disconnected during a game ). If you were playing versus AI, the game state is saved. If you were playing versus a human, you have to try and login as soon as possible, otherwise the computer will pass your turn within seconds. The developers have been working on this game for 4 years, so it's a bit odd that this problem exists but I'm sure that given time, the problem will be rectified.

This is stealth gaming at its purest. Lurk in the shadows, climb in the rafters, and only approach enemies when there's no one to hear them scream. The combat is unweildy, awkward, and just plain bad - and that makes it amazing. If fighting were viable, or even enjoyable, it would ruin the game's incredible tension. And the tension in the game is incredible - so thick you could cut it with a nasty serrated dagger. The levels are immense and superbly designed, feeling wholly natural while offering a smorgasbord of finely-tuned stealth challenges. On top of that, there are so many routes through each environment that you can replay them time and again and still discover new things. The excellence of the design is further exemplified by later missions, which see you doing the same levels backwards (with new enemy patrols). Exfiltrating the same tightly-guarded spot you just worked so hard to get into has an entirely different feel to it, and makes the environments feel all the more real.
Fans of "Of Orcs and Men" know how good the story in that game was, and Styx delivers on the same level. At first it seems a little generic - bit of amnesia here, bit of "dark fantasy" language there - but when the pieces start to fall into place it reveals itself to be an intelligent and thought-provoking examination of a lot of heavy concepts.
Styx: Master of Shadows is the best stealth game I've played in years, and I play a LOT of stealth games. If you're sick of the namby-pamby handholding that characterizes stuff like Assassin's Creed, this could easily be one of your new favourite games.

Impossible Creatures magically recreates my youth in 1930s Nebraska. From the cheetahs with lobster claws to the chimpanzees with lobster claws, everything I remember about lobster claws is there. In fact, it includes many animals I didn't realize had no lobster claws. I know some of my childhood friends (who had no lobster claws themselves) traded rumors about hammerhead sharks without lobster claws, but all the hammerheads I saw from my beach villa had lobster claws. The musk oxen grazing along the beach didn't have lobster claws, thankfully -- otherwise we'd have needed to reinforce all our homes with lobster claws cast in gold. Musk oxen were always charging buildings, but they didn't cause much harm because they didn't have lobster claws, which greatly increase the damage inflicted on buildings. Getting back to hammerhead sharks, I learned that they sometimes possess primate forelimbs (in lieu of lobster claws), and they can hurl small rocks a considerable distance. Despite their excellent vision radius, the giraffes with lobster claws were never able to throw things very well because lobster claws are not suited to ballistic activity. Speaking of giraffes, if you ever come across one with a lupine torso, don't bother running. It's got crazy endurance and will be in tip-top shape when you're panting and wheezing and collapsed on the ground. Even though it has no lobster claws, the giraffe can easily stomp you with its hooves or maul you with its non-lobster claws. Be very careful around giraffes, their appetite for the flesh of creatures without lobster claws is insatiable. Unless you have lobster claws yourself, then you're probably safe.
In short, all my lobster claw nostalgia is satisfied with this lobster claw simulator.
FULL DISCLOSURE: I don't have lobster claws.

Wanted to like this game, had high hopes, but this game was a resounding disappointment. Lets start off with the game setup. The art is nice, so is how "open" it is and there is a lot to collect. The story seems interesting and there are a lot of bosses.
Now the bad. The way the game is setup is with this giant map with tons of different vertical platforms and interconnected levels. There is also no real map, markings, information, quest markers, or anything. Quests give you no information, besides potentially tell you a direction to go in or maybe a specific area to get them, or maybe even neither of those. Don't mind that the map doesn't have the whole world, nor does it label anything. This leads to wandering a round and wasting hours on end with no idea what to do. This has led the community to create a map, and tons of people posting how they are lost because of no direction or information given by the game. Then, since every level has tons of different platforms and is super vertical, but has doors, levels, magic walls, it is impossible to get to half the stuff. I get some people love the "metroid" style but it basically is just backtracking, having to remember a wall you saw 3 hours about that you now have a power for. You never know where to get anything, or what to do with it.
You collect a bunch of team members but they don't seem to do anything nor does the game tell you what to do. You have tons of inventory spots, and levels of abilities, but the game doesn't give you any information about them either. I played for hours and still had tons of empty spaces in my inventory. The item system works by you basically collect a bunch of random mats that drop and you trade in a bunch for one thing. This means to get 1 thing you need 15 different types of mats, and if every single one hasn't dropped you don't get it. So instead of actually getting things, you're left with 1/2 the required amount needed of mats in your inventory without getting anything new ever. I used the same chestpiece for the whole time, because nothing I picked up was better.
Then theres the terrible platforming. The controls are way too finnicky and floaty. Sometimes you guy will grab a ledge, other times he won't. Sometimes he will wall jump, sometimes he wont. If you use the analog when you jump you will slide off. Then there is the dash and the ground slam. They are done by using the directional buttons, instead of a button, wich would make more sense. This means tons of times when you want to jump, just because you touched down, you will slam down to the ground. Or you will suddenly dash without wanting to, just because of their terrible control scheme. Other times your guy won't jump soon enough when you press it, or he will just slide off the ledge. The controls are anything but tight, which you would expect for a game like this. Then, in annoying poorly done fashion, if you get hit there is the terrible "I must be interrupted and go flying backwards for no reason" which means while you are jumping or on a ledge if you get hit all and fall back or off a platform, which is frustrating when it shouldn't be.The game utilizes way too many timed mechanic puzzles just to open doors or get chests. Every area has, unlock 3 things in a row with 0 margin of error just to get an item you won't use, or a single mat.
The combat is pretty bad too, because each hit stuns you, you can get constantly chained and juggled by 2-3 normal enemies who just with continually hit you with no cooldown while you keep getting stunned. Not to mention they do tons of damage. In 1 group of regular guys I lost 2/3 my health in 2 second stun chain, which is soo dumb. The dash in combat is super finnicky too. There are guys that you can't walk past, who have shields you can't attack from in front. If you try and jump over they just slash up in the air and with the questionable hitboxes you will get hit no matter what. This means you must dash past them. But you can only dash once because for some reason it needs a cooldown. If you aren't exactly right up next to them you won't go through them. This means youll stand in front of them and they will just be able to hit you because you can't get past them for some reason, and dashin is dumb.
Then there are the boss fights. Most of them are more annoying than they are fun. You never know when they are coming. You suddenly enter a room and the boss fight started, meaning if you don't have potions you are screwed. You cannot leave the area either if you don't want to fight. And since you only can restore potions in the 1 save checkpoint per giant area you will unlikely be able to do it. Some guys use almost instant kill attacks that you can get caught in like a fire pillar.Many people on the discussion forums talk about all the different annoying cheap boss fights that weren't fun, so there are many ones. I fought a stupid annoying boss that you can't hurt until you climb a bunch of platforms while doddging homing swords, to destroy a crystal, so you can then hurt him, but your magic and weapons do very little damage, and once the crystal heals itself it then will heal the boss. This means I made almost no progress and there was nothing I could do about it. Each time I would do about 1/20th of his health after he was healed.
Then theres the spells. Instead of being easy to use, they are triggered to holding R trigger and ALSO pressing a directional key. So you have to remember which spell is related to which directional preference, also, since they are directional, this causes problems with movements and dash/slam. Many times I would go to cast a spell and it would make me move off a ledge, or instead of casting it would make me use a cancel/slam. Also, there are different types of spells :light/dark/fire/ice. The problem is is some do no damage to enemies and others are weak to some. This means in each area, you have to figure out what each guy is, and what they are weak to, then switch your spells to them on the wheeel, which isn't easy to do as its finnicky when using the quick/change ability. Add to it that some abilities you need to get up to ledges or through doors and it becomes annoying. You somehow level up abilities but that isn't explained nor didn't seem to happen much. You level up, but only get to add 1 attibute point total, and the abilities in the tree you choose from are boring, like 10% more health, crits deal more damage, you deal more damage in 5 chain hits, etc, and the higher level abilities can only be gotten once you get a level, but ALSO once you get 2 different abilities that form a tree to that ability, meaning you will have to waste points in things you don't want to get something later on.
The way the open-endedness is done is just terrible. Sure there is tons of things to unlock and a big map to explore, but the levels have 5 ways to go, are super vertical and annoying to navigate through, there is no real fastravel (besides btw 3 villages), no markers/waypoints, no maps, no information about anything at all. For this main quest, I was supposed to go into these 2 different areas, but one of them required a key that I didn't have. Why would the main quest send me to somehwere I can't go. Apparently I was just supposed to wander around a ton or fight some random boss or do something random to get that key. The other area had this annoying healing boss I did no damage to. From watching videos some guys did tons of damage with the same spells that I used that did none, but my spells were level 1. So apparently either this video guy was too high level or I was supposed to level up my spells, but how I don't know. I either had to grind levels or find some random area/ optional boss that helped me level them up. There are new weapons and abilities to get, but you need to find the random chest/puzzle/optional boss/teammate instead of natural progression.

Valdis Story is gorgeous, has an awesome soundtrack, and features combat similar to Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, and Devil May Cry. The world is laid out in a similar way to Super Metroid, with many atmospheric and highly stylized zones to explore.
You can sink many hours into this game, since Valdis Story encourages you to do multiple playthroughs. Each character's playstyle is different, which creates a unique experience each time. For completionists, God Slayer difficulty is a genuine challenge, especially if you're trying to get "S Rank" during each of the boss encounters. Not an easy task, because boss difficulty ranges from total pushover to insanely tough.
Similar to Diablo's skill tree system, each character has three unique skill trees, featuring unlockable special moves and bonuses. You earn stat points as you level up, and your character has a primary stat which they're built around. Fortunately, you can also respec your character's skills by visiting a vendor (Mesmer), which I felt was a nice touch. You won't get locked into one skill tree.
Playing as Vladyn (unlockable character):
Vladyn's arsenal of guns provides long range attacks, and his summonable minions will jump straight into combat, while absorbing tons of damage. Unlike some of the melee characters, Vladyn can rack up gigantic combos from across the screen, especially with his Long Gun (Rifle) and Doombringer (Launcher). He's a hell of a lot of fun! You can unlock him by finishing the game once, along with Gilda (heavy magic user).
Critique:
My one complaint about Valdis story has to do with its jumping puzzles and level designs, which can lead to frustrating situations and/or deaths. Sometimes, your character is knocked off a ledge by an enemy, and you'll fall multiple floors back towards the start of the area. On other occasions, you'll just barely get grazed by enemies who cast status effect spells (Fire, Poison, Lightning), and your character "locks up" temporarily, and becomes stunned. Thankfully, even if you die, Save Points are fairly common.
On harder difficulties, you'll get punished for not blocking or evading enemy attacks. Getting hit multiple times can absolutely mess up your timing, and it'll also result in you dying very quicky. In this way, Valdis Story plays a bit like a fighting game. Practice blocking and Skill Canceling, and you'll be good to go, even against some of the scarier bosses.
It's a good idea to purchase armor/trinkets which reduce/nullify status effects. Thankfully, the Paladin Armor and Armor of the Grey Knight provide status immunities. Equipping powerful weapons and items can make all the difference in this game.
Arena mode (NEW!)
The newly updated version of the game (featuring Arena mode) adds a new dimension to Valdis Story, and it's also perfect for testing different builds of each character. Arena mode is tough, and you'll find yourself facing multiple bosses all at once. Good luck, you'll need it.
Final Score: 9/10

This game is, in a nutshell, a post Igarashi-era Castlevania. It's a very beautiful game, both graphically and musically, with soothing piano scores. In many regards, it's a well done game. But there's just so much I have to nitpick.
Valdis Story tells the story of a young man fighting the likes of angels and demons. His ship is destroyed and he sets out to rescue his homies. I actually liked the setting and story elements, I just wish there was more of it. There wasn't really enough dialogue to develop any characters.
The boss battles are intense and in many cases, gimmicky. These were great. Though if you completely lacked certain things, like spell upgrades, some bosses were perhaps way too hard.
Here are some features I would have liked to see or change.
-The inability to duck is baffling, and my number one complaint. Hitting down is defaulted to slide/cancel. While you can unbind this, on more than one occasion I find myself unintentionally moving forward while "crouching forward" because I expect the ability to duck to halt horizontal movement.
-There are a few leaps of faith in the game, where you cannot guess where you will land with no way to get back up the same way. Some means to see a little further ahead would help.
-Having attacks lunge my character forward tends to make me move all over the place, which is problematic on certain bosses that I try to fight near ledges.
-The prevalence of near-perfect timed jumps is overkill. A few jump puzzles are great, but not every area needs one, let alone two.
-The lack of a unified world map makes navigation surprisingly difficult, despite the fantastic mini-map. Even after beating it twice, I still don't really have a feel for the layout.
-Related to the above, backtracking is somewhat high because it's difficult to tell where to go.
-Bouncing back when hit is fine, but the extremely short invulnerability period makes this problem outstanding. The repeated loss of control is aggravating.
-Status afflictions such as stun last a long time, considering this is a solo real-time adventure.
-Normal difficulty is still too punishing. Yeah it's doable, but it's not nice at all to new players to the genre. An easier difficulty would be a welcome addition.
-A high-speed movement ability would be nice for end-game exploration, given the large amount of backtracking.
-Inability to block heavy attacks by default seems counter-intuitive. It's not like players automatically know what a heavy attack looks like.
-A curious amount of grinding is required for a completionist type player who wants every item upgraded. By the end of the game I had very few things upgraded.
-The library, which seems like it'd be the perfect hub to hang out and reach other areas, is oddly out-of-the-way of just about everything.
-Certain crew members are almost too important to miss out on, such as every upgrader. These characters should instead be unable to be missed.
-Boss battles are completely unannounced. If you walked into that next room with next to no health and a far away save point, good luck beating it.
-Also there's no quick option to restart bosses. You must resort to suicide or returning to the menu.
Valdis Story is a very commendable game to be accomplished with such a small team. It looks great, it sounds great, it plays okayish. In the end, all i'm really asking for is a more forgiving easy diffulty. There's a pretty good amount of replay value, with several unlockable characters who play quite differently, but I couldn't bring myself to sit through the game one more time. I feel this game deserves a 7.5. Thanks chicago!

Ooh. Tough one. This game's biggest issue is lack of content. The only reason I have any substantial playtime is because I'm a completion freak, but otherwise... there's not much there. 13 levels, all of them can be cleared pretty quickly and none of the puzzles are terriby mind-boggling. There are only 4 different pencil types too, pencils being the main puzzle-solvers in the game, and their uses are fairly limited, so it becomes repetitive pretty quickly. Worst of all is that you don't really need to draw anything at all. The main character can be squiggles. Fire is squiggles. A /key/ is squiggles. It doesn't matter in the slightest, though with how imprecise the drawing element is anyways maybe that's for the better. Oh by the way if you die in a level (and you die quick) have fun redoing the entire thing! With how tedious some of the levels are, dying for dumb reasons (the majority of all deaths) take it from boring to frustrating. And it's not even a hard game...
The graphics look alright, the music is okay though there aren't too many tracks and it's not much above MIDI quality most of the time. The game isn't terribly interesting though and certainly doesn't warrant EPIC in the title.

Gunpoint was one of the first indie games that caught my attention on Steam, and boy did it deliver.
It is a 2D stealth platformer, and a minimalist version of what Watch Dogs should have been. Much of the gameplay revolves around rewiring circuitry within buildings in order to confuse guards, drop them through pits, electrocute them, and whatever else is necessary in order to reach the objective and get out without being seen. If you are seen, you get shot in the face with perfect accuracy, and it's reload time. Either you're sneaky, or you're dead, and there are no ifs, ands, or buts about it. As you complete more missions, you can improve your abilities (e.g. how fast and far you can jump), with more tools becoming available to navigate the traps that protect those computers that are just waiting to be hacked.
There is a campaign to follow, with dialog that is much better than expected and quite funny for your average millenial. You work as a private investigator and get caught up in a web of intrigue, which is entertaining to follow, but by no means  a big selling point.
The game is about 5 hours long, and every mission quite rewarding to play and explore how to quickly finish as you are being graded on how quickly the mission is solved. After the campaign is finished, you get access to a super upgrade that lets you kick down doors, so you can blast through the entire game in record time and show those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ guards who's boss.
Overall, it's a fun little game to play, and easy to just jump in and play. There is no need to fear the usual slog that comes with becoming invested in a game, as you can just go in and play a mission here or there, or just mow down the entire 5 hour campaign. I recommend it with a 8/10 rating. It's good and cheap enough to buy full price, and is fantastic value at a steam sale.

Gunpoint is a simple, yet challenging game that blends stealth gameplay with heavy puzzle elements and vintage noir aesthetics. The end result is a entertaining game full of clever mechanics, level design, and writing.
Rewiring an entire electrical system to deliver a high voltage shock to a guard is immensely satisfying, yet so is sneaking around them all entirely with them being none the wiser, or even simply punching them in the face until the game itself expresses its distrubance at your apparent lack of restraint.
Beyond finding creative ways to assault security personel, the lasting appeal of Gunpoint is finding new and interesting ways of navigating its various challenges. The visuals are expressive, the soundtrack is fantastic, and the writing is consistently hilarious. My one complaint is that the game itself is rather short, but it does have quite a bit of replay value and a level editor, so there is plenty of content to enjoy outside the main story.

Pretty impressive, actually. Very easy to understand, with solid tutorials and really swell community base on their website. Incredible support too - no canned response bullcrap.
Creating a game is as easy as adding sprites, tilesheets, sounds and such on the layout. The interface is intuitive enough to learn, understand and use quickly. Want to bring it together? As long as you understand simple game logic - hell, as long as you understand logic - you'll get a good grasp of its Events system and you'll be programming in no time. And, it ships out with templates and a few game demos to get you started as soon as you install.
The tutorials are from their site, and are very comprehensive and user-friendly. Prepare to make your first simple game literally minutes after finishing the tutorial.
The forums are well moderated, and the people are as friendly as they can get. Loads of content there, too, ranging from plugins to game content you might want to try for your game.
Support for this product is also A+.  Very polite, and resolves issues FAST, with no dilly-dallying. They even answered my questions promptly BEFORE I purchased. Really nice.
But it's not perfect. One downside is that it's not a 'buy-one-get-all' package - expect to download several more programs or plugins for doing sprites and music, More of a minor nuiscance, really, with loads of royalty-free content online. Another one is that there's no Linux version.
You have two purchase options for the Personal/Business license: here on Steam, or at the developer's storefront. Well, the Steam version does have DRM, so... you have a choice.
But, considering everything, you'll want this if you're into 2D game development. An easy-to-use interface coupled with great support from the developers and community is hook enough for me. I bought my license from the developer's storefront itself during their January sale at 33% off (so no DRM), but if you want to grab the Steam version (at 50% off during sale), by all means, do so. Either way, I'm sure you'll never regret it.

I was bored last weekend and figured I'd give an EA game another shot.  After clocking ten hours in three or so days, I must say I am impressed with the amount of content so far.  Think minecraft alpha after the redstone update.  There is no electricity yet so that might have been a bad analogy but still, the content is enough for the time being.
Plenty of different blocks and you can turn them into different shapes to meet your building needs.  No, I'm not talking stairs, pyramids and squares, I'm talking rounded corners and a myriad of other different curved shapes.  This can let you build that tower you always wanted but got hosed by minecrafts limitations.  I shouldn't really compare this to minecraft, it's just in the same genre not the same game.  Yes you mine, you build, and you eat to survive but that is where the similarities end.  You build tables with different variants and colors depending on what you want.  You cna go medieval or you can go modern or a mix of both.  Plenty of different blocks like marble, stone, cobblestone, sandstone, loam, metal, wood, the list goes on.
Biomes were introduced last month based on the update news.  So far I've seen the temperate, tundra, and safari.  I took an axe to an elephant and got wrecked.  Bears...well get a weapon to say the least.  Mountains and ditches as well as caves and ravines are plentiful.  Penguins, moose, chicken, sheep, bear, cows, pigs, giraffe, and elephants galore.  I managed to dig down far enough after a few days of playing to get to hell.  The only place that a liquid exists.  Word of advice, don't fall in, it's easy to do.
Outside of those features there are a crap ton of ores.  Copper, iron, silver, gold, tungsten, mithril, cobalt, and aluminum.   Some of these don't have any apparent use yet but they are working on that.  Water is presumeably the next update as well.  This should make getting something to drink in the game easier as right now you eat apples or watermelon to get rehydrated.
The music is very ambient and sporadic.  Everything seems to flow and I haven't glitched to my death yet.  You can rotate things you are about to place as well as even out the land whether it be dirt or solid rock.  Nothing like a sledgehammer to make that wall flat!  I started a tomato farm but haven't really went beyond that.
For a game that has been out for as long as it has, I was expecting more.  However, there is still plenty to do and build.  I'm not sure how many more world wipes will  be necessary but it isn't a big deal as I enjoy building in this game.
Multiplayer works well.  You can host straight off of your computer to jump right in or you can host a dedicated server.  This can be either on a separate box or it can be one that you pay for in the event you are not network savvy ro simply don't have the capability to host a server for whatever reason.  At the current time I give this game a thumbs up.  Time will tell but I think with the constant support and active development team, this could turn into a masterpiece.  Just keep in mind this is still an alpha build.

Phantom Breaker: Battle Grounds is a fun side-scrolling beat 'em up game where you smash your way through waves of enemies and stage bosses. You have a choice of (initially) four different weaponized girls of varying degrees of moe. You gain levels which persist between playthroughs, encouraging even newbies to improve their characters over time.
The game's main flaws include a confusing set of keyboard controls (which can't seem to be changed) and the lack of an online multiplayer mode (which seems to be in development, but long overdue).
Overall, the game is worth trying out for those who are looking for a more relaxed and lighthearted beat 'em up game.

This game reminds me of the first Thief game. There is very little hand holding and you can take several routes to achieve your goal. Throw in some odd abilities like creating a clone of yourself and using it to face hug a guard while you slip past, and you end up with a fun game that feels open and interesting.
I'm about halfway through the game now and have already gone back to try different tactics through a couple of levels.  I've seen a few comments on difficult controls, but I disagree. I like the fact that I have to land a jump or grab ledge instead of the game automatically performing the action for me because I held down a couple of buttons. There is no automatic parkour action. Also, your inventory is limited. So you're forced to vary your abilities and hunt for replacement items when you run out.
I like the storyline so far and the voice acting is pretty good. Especially considering the price. If I have one complaint it would be that the cursing in the game seems forced. Almost like they added it just to have it in there. I noticed the same thing in Of Orcs and Men as well.
I definitely recommend getting this if you enjoy older style stealth games. I hope they make another.

Also it has a maid who smashes stuff with an oversized anime hammer. Because of course it does.

I'm a fan of stealth games, being somewhat patient and never one to run and gun.  Styx: Master of Shadows is an enjoyable stealth game for the price.  What I like about it is the sense of it being different: you are a goblin in a world of men; not a second class or even a third class citizen: you are a monster.  And yet Styx, the protagonist, is not the evil creature that goblins are so often portrayed as in common fantasy...he is an anti-hero, but not vile.
I liked the style of the game: the castle settings are very intricate: it's a maze of tunnels, stairways, balconies, ledges, etc...if you like climbing and skulking and choosing the best path, you will enjoy this game.
I found the stealth mechanic to be fairly balanced...you have to be careful: they will see you if you are too close, even if it is in the shadows, so you reallly have to time your movements...and if you kick over a bucket, you will arouse suspicion and the guards will quickly investigate.
If you are looking for Assassin's Creed combat, you will not find it here, in the least...combat is about timing your parries to block strikes from the guards; if you do it poorly, the hits will take a massive chunk of heath out.  If you do it well, and block two parries, this will "unbalance" the guard and your next move will be a simple kill move (at least in the beginning levels).
Two words: avoid combat.  You will live longer.
Kills, if you have to, are  made from behind...remember, you are  strong, but you are a goblin the size of a five year old or   something similar, in a world of heavily armored and armed guards.
What I don't like is the vagueness of the plot: Styx needs to steal the Heart of the Tree, and I really don't know why yet...
Also, the ledge detection takes some getting used to, but I think that I'm getting the hang of it after dying cheaply from casual leaps to what should have been safety, but turned out to be plunges into the abyss...
Sound effects are detailed and good; you need to be able to hear what is going on to know what to avoid.
Music is atmospheric and well suited to the game.
I recommend this game, especially for the price.

I'm a sucker for good stealth games, and this one hits the spot. It's definitely a challenge -- Thief-style map (i.e. has no "you are here" marker), lots of objects to accidentally knock over, limited inventory and highly-sensitive guard AI. The highlight of the game for me is that there are
of ways to make your way from Point A to Point B in this game; There doesn't seem to be a "golden path", or even "alternative paths" -- you feel as if you're forging your own path every time. On a related note, the levels are enormous, and the level design is fantastic (in my opinion). Environment/world design is interesting and pleasing to the eye as well.
There are a few significant flaws, which might be a dealbreaker for some: dialogue and storyline are lackluster, graphics are nothing to write home about (Unreal 3), combat is clunky (but do you
want to be getting into combat?), NPC AI is kind of dumb most of the time (but predictable, at least -- also, I saw in the credits that they only had one poor soul working on AI... that sucks!), and Assassin's Creed-esque ledge-grabbing doesn't always work the way you want it to. Also, I had the same complaint about Dishonored, but the "stats" screen that shows number of kills, number of people alerted, etc., only comes up at very end of each multi-part level. That can be really painful when you're trying achieve a "no alert, no kill" run.
Despite the game's flaws, Styx: Master of Shadows is exactly what the doctor ordered, and has some serious replayability value. Definitely worth the price.

Alrighty, let me get the short version of this out of the way.
Is the game good? YES
Does the game have problems? YES
Do I think these problems make the game unplayable? NO
What did I like about this game? It's aesthetic is pleasing to the eye, the music is catchy although I will admit it gets lost sometimes behind dozens of sword slashes, guys going "OOF!" in pain, girls going "OOH!" in pain, and your character's battle cries on top of it. I also find the combat simple, if enjoyable. Granted I haven't played the longest ammount of time and therefore might not know all there is to know, but right now it just seems like you need one button for your basic combos, with other buttons only starting later on the combo string, and a couple other buttons for blocking and special moves.
What don't I like? Well I have to admit the learning curve is a tiny bit high. I'm not saying that it needs a condescending tutorial saying "press this to do this, etc.", but some simple prompts or tips might be useful. I didn't even know you could leap between background and foreground until the very tail end of the 1st level. Before then, I was just staring in confusion as I would wait long periods wondering why a single enemy didn't come to fight me. It was just that I had to go fight him. Again, a tiny bit of clarity or explanation would go a long way in this game. I hear there are issues with controller support at the moment. Sadly I cannot find my controller to test this, and do not have anybody at home to try the local co-op either. I do wish that the online co-op was fixed and implemented, this game cries for a person to play with and sometimes local is just too clumsy.
Do not be afraid to experiment in this game. Also, fair warning to new players, the pie throwing enemies in stage 1 (second level you play) will be a pain to fight if you don't know the system and can find a workaround to their tactics.  Another hint, get the combo upgrades early, if you're an attack happy kinda guy, the combo upgrades are a godsend.
Overall, I enjoy this game. I believe I got it as part of a humble bundle so I got it a bit cheaper, but for $12 I'd say there are worse games for you to buy out there. Not the best but not bad by a long shot, especially if you're in the mood for a good hack n' slash. It's a solid recommendation that becomes a terrific recommendation if you pick it up during a sale or a bundle, like I did.
