Overall, I think this is one of the better side-scrolling beat 'em ups. The art style is fantastic, the music is nice and it fits the levels, the characters are appealing and there are a lot of enemies to fight. The story mode isn't very long, I'd say you could finish it in about 2 hours or so.
There are five difficulties, ranging from Easy to Nightmare+. The game overall isn't very hard though, in my opinion. It's not really difficult to get huge combos, since most of the time the enemies just stand around, waiting to get attacked. It's really satisfying to get a huge combo though, so I guess that's not a huge problem for me. These different difficulties do add replayability to the game, which I supposed is nice.
One thing I really liked about this game was the 2-lane system. Basically, there are 2 lanes you can fight in, the front lane and the back lane. This makes the flow of the game a lot faster, because otherwise all enemies would get jammed into one small area. There are some bigger enemies in this game that you can't jump over, so in my opinion, this is a great solution.
Not everything in this game is that good though. The story felt a bit slapped on. I didn't really feel like I was saving anyone, I was just beating up enemies for the fun of it. I think the story could've touched a bit more on the enemies themselves. I'm pretty sure it said somewhere in the beginning of the game that they were robots, but don't quote me on that. I would've loved to know a bit more than that though. Exactly why did I have to fight all those robots. The areas could've been explained a bit better as well. Why was I fighting in those spots? You fight on beaches, in a cafetaria, in some parking spot. But why those locations? That's would like to know.
About the controls: The keyboard controls are not as tight as they should be. I spent the first few minutes of the game just mashing my keyboard to figure out the controls. The game doesn't clearly explain the controls, some kind of tutorial would've been nice. It expects you to play with a controller, but I currently don't have one, so I had to use my keyboard. For anyone who wants to know, these are the basic controls.
W: Jump (Double tap to double jump)
S: Duck
A: Move left (Double tap and hold to sprint)
D: Move right (Double tap and hold to sprint)
J: Quick attack
B: Heavy attack
U: Use a combo
There are more buttons and combinations you can use, but those are the basics you need to play the game.
You need to collect XP in every stage to level up. After you clear the stage, you earn some points you can spend on either unlocking new skills or upgrading your attack/defence/speed. It's impossible to fully complete both your skill tree and your stats though, as the cap is set at level 50. After that, you do not level up anymore, so you don't earn more points to level up. This is a good thing though, because otherwise you would get ridiculously overpowered characters that can beat even Nightmare+ with ease.
TL;DR
Here's a small list of pros and cons for this game.
Pros:
-Great levels and character design
-The music is nice
-Enjoyable 2-lane system
-A lot of characters with different combos to choose from
-The game has a lot of replayability
Cons:
-Bad keyboard controls
-Story mode is kind of short
-Story overall isn't that good
I recommend this game, but not for the full €11,99. Try to buy it in a sale, then this game is worth it for sure.

Oh hey, an objective based zombie game where you plant a bomb and escape while fighting through hordes of zombies. It's as if Counter-Strike and Left 4 Dead had a baby.
The gameplay is alright, and it's enough to have some fun with your friends. You can choose 5 classes, each having their own weapons and equipment ranging from shotguns, SMGs, grenades, supply boxes and turrets. You go through each level shooting zombies, planting a bomb then getting the hell out of there. Each class fills a different role and teamwork  can get you out of the worst possible situations. Zombies spawn randomly and there are crescendo events like in Left 4 Dead where hordes of zombies keep coming at you, and they aren't as fragile as the L4D common infected.
Combat in this game is simple, your class carries a primary and secondary gun (usually pistols) and you can shoot from the hip (automatic weapons have quite a bit of recoil) and aim down the sights which eliminates recoil but makes you move slower. You can also melee bash the zombies, and from what I know it one hit kills normal zombies on Casual and Average.
The visuals are... eh. They're mod quality, and I DO NOT mean that in a good way. Honestly, it looks as if it were made years ago and you see HL2 assets (which is alright I guess) and I literally recognize most of the gun models from M9K and GDCW weapon packs from Garry's Mod. At least you'll most likely be able to run this game well.
Variety is meh... there are currently 4 maps in rotation each with different paths/objective spots, and there are two types of enemies. Regular zombies, your standard slow but hard hitting zombies and armored zombies and they sometimes drop supplies. Sorta like in Left 4 Dead 2.
The music is... eh... listen to it and you'll see what I mean.
As a bonus, the menu also has a built in direct connect and it's own create server window with your basic options for the server, not just the default one. It even tells you what port to forward if you're into that, so good on you developers.
Would I be mad if I paid for this? Yeah, I probably would, but it's free, and its enough fun to have a good session with your friends. Also it's Early Access, so for all I know, there could be more zombies and maps and the game could look and play much better in the future.

(Not sure what happened to my earlier review, so here's a reiteration:)
This game suffers from:
1. Lousy User Interface.
2. No tutorial
3. Lacking core things that should have been implemented before leaving Early Access [like an options menu] not in the game yet,
4. Plenty of bugs, poor syncing, and crashing
5. No server population, and given its stability issues, you may run into trouble just trying to run with friends
6: Few roles implemented, only a single randomized free-for-all-style mode implemented
On the flip side, the gameplay was fun- though it seemed a bit imbalanced and is clearly designed with more, rather than less players in mind.
It's not a bad game, just one that left EA too early and lacks in population.
If it's ever stabilized and fleshed out, and if you manage to grab some friends for it, it could be a good time.
As far as gameplay:
Static map layout, but room contents change each load-up
Your role is selected at start. Each role has different room interactables and shop purchases.
All characters move at the same speed, so pinning people or cornering them into traps is key, but that's impossible with too few players [nevermind all the teleporting and failed contact recognition and so forth the game suffers from].
Honestly, as fun as a game as it is, it's lacking depth for long term play, and when you factor in the incomplete nature of it, it's incredibly hard to recommend.
Plus side, it dropped in price to $1, and steam refunds exist, so by all means, give it a shot and decide for yourself. :)

I tried to play this game a year ago, but put it into my 'early access' category even though it wasn't labeled as such because it was obviously unfinished. Shortly after that a new patch came out adding the final boss (see what I mean about early access?), and there hasn't been another update in nearly a year since. The game would still be enjoyable in its current state if not for some particularly rough edges. Most important among them, the game lacks immunity frames, so if you hit certain types of traps or get hit by certain attacks, you'll lose your entire life bar in a single hit (which is really a dozen hits landing all at once). Given the current state of the game I can't tell if that's a bug or by design, but it's terrible either way. Add onto that some extremely unbalanced bosses that make you feel underleveled even at max level, and the game just isn't any fun after awhile. It feels punishing in a very unfair way.
I'd say wait for an update before getting this game, but I've been waiting a year and it still feels like early access. Maybe get it on a deep discount, but full price is too much until they at least fix some of the more glaring issues.

Warhammer 40.000: Dawn of War II is a sequel to Warhammer 40.000: Dawn of War, and gives you a new story, with new Characters. The Commander have no real name, only the name you give him.
It starts out with the war against Orcs and Elders, but you will face a greater thread, The tyranids.
The Tyranids are a dinosaur like alien race, with the strategy; Numbers over Strength.
You control only Hero units in the story, The Commander, Tarkus (Normal Marine with 4 in squad), Cyrus(Scout/Sniper with 3 in squad), Avitus(Heavy Weapon with 3 is squad), Thaddeus(Melee Jetpack with 4 in squad) and Gordian(Support).
You play as the Blood Ravens in a war to free the world from The Tyranids and with equipment you can find in the stages and equip after the battle gives the game more depth and with level up system and skill tree, you can make the ultimate team.
The Chaos Rising Expansion, follows up after the war on Tyranids and put you against the Chaos Space Marines.
There is also Retribution. The worse Expansion ever.
You can choose what race you want to play, in the campaign, but the battles are the same, only different Rival.
Warhammer 40.000: Dawn of War II is a pretty well made game with pretty good story, and with the different gamemodes it makes it more fun.

Excellent Metroidvania mixed with Hack&Slash and RPG elements.
At the moment of this review, only 2 characters are out, while other 2 are being developed. Even without those 2, the game is extremely good.
The characters playstyles have a lot of depth as well. Depending on how you build them you have a lot of different approaches. You could sneak up on enemies, or hit them hard with your magics, you could be an extremely agile character, running back and forth hitting your enemies, or simply facetank them.
The skill system provides unique synergies, some more obvious than others, and the playable characters have a few different weapons you can use, each having their unique combos, ranging from lightning fast attacks, to slow and hard hitting, and even some with special quirks like long range attacks or granting buffs to yourself via combos.
On top of the playable characters, part of the game is finding your crew, which provide you with support. You can summon some to attack your enemies and buff yourself, while others grants you techniques, upgrade your gear or simply function as extra shops.
And you are going to need all that help. The bosses are pretty tough, perhaps even too tough at first glance, however, if you learn how to dodge and block, you'll find them very rewarding when you get a high score.

I bought this game during the 2017 Steam Summer Sale, so my review will reflect it having been a lower price, although I would not recommend this game at the discounted price either.
So this game, to start, enticed me with its charming art style and varied yet fitting music. It sets you up as a janitor at this spaceport that is doomed to pick up trash every day for what seems like forever. This is a really novel concept, one that understandably won't interest everyone: Who wants to play as a janitor? Well, its possible to have monotonous or "boring" jobs become good games, such as Paper's Please, so if that idea doesn't exactly vibe well with you I'd pass on this game.
Each day starts the same but for some reason the developers don't really give you a solid grasp on what to do, atleast convieniently. Most of the stuff you pick is trash but some of it can be sold, rarely will it be a good price. You need the money to get food in order to go to sleep to wake up to burn trash and sell trash to get money to get food to go to sleep ..........This is what every day wil be like, and the only guide you have in this is a journal that leaves much to be desired. It tells you a general idea of what to do but boils down to : Burn Trash, Eat, and Sleep.
Thematically I understand the meaning and commentary going on but when playing it it just doesn't work. The monotony of cleaning this place up is fun for the first few days but you realize eveyday is exactly the same. You need to find items during your money making trash pickups. The items you need to get are so rare to find on the ground, and are often expensive as hell at whatever merchant stand has them. Which you'd think would be easy, but besides the fact that all items in the game change where they are sold, by who they are sold, how much they are sold for, there's ALOT of merchants in this game. They are divided into different quarters that will roughly organize items, but taking out the obvious examples (weapons go to the adventuring quarter), you'll find your self asking where you should even start to look for the right merchant. This alone is annoying but is made worse by the spaceport itself.
It is a very beautiful place but it is unbearably terrbile to play in. It's confusing to walk in and despite about 4 hours of gametime at the time of this review I still have trouble putting together a map of the place. Because you don't get a mini map or map for your journal, good luck. The closest thing I got to a "map" was a display or diorama of the space port in the dungeons which is essentially useless because its large and can't be taken with you. I read some of the discussions for this game and some people argue that you should keep playing and just get a sense of the spaceport, that getting lost is "part of the expereince". I could agree if the spaceport was different for each person, like procedurally generated or shifted as the day goes on, but instead of being designed to be cleverly disorienting this game comes off more as pointlessly complex. While this mirrors a big city atmosphere, so it works thematically, it isn't fun to play in nor is it challenging. The game doesn't ask you to "get good", it requires you get used to its awkward and clumsy choices.
Additionally there are a few areas that seem pointless to go to, and when I walked through them it felt like I should have been elsewhere looking for stuff to do.
Not that there is much to do besides pick up trash. You can go into the dungeons, which I thought would be more prominent in this game, as in something you do more often, but it amounts to nothing as well.
I think that's the problem with "Diaries of a Spaceport Janitor", that there doesn't feel like any reason to get things done because you don't feel any payoff for your actions. You can't upgrade your trash incinerator to have a bigger battery, you can't upgrade your backpack to hold more stuff, you can't make the prices in the town go down significantly, you can't customize your house or character or space port. I didn't feel as if I accomplished anything in this game in the time that I played it, and it was frustrating to know that after all the time I spent it didn't matter. This cute world didn't change for better or worse despite what I did.
Another point other gamers brought up in the discussion forums was how this game is a simulation, so its slower pace and goals are justified by being an experience and not merely a game. However there are ways to make simulations fun, and one of the best ways to make a simulation fun is to give a meaningful story that meshes with an equally developed game. "Diaries of a Spaceport Janitor" does not give you one. While your character does face discrimination that highlights how they feel, such as being abused by the police type NPC's and cat-called on the streets by creepy aliens, you don't feel a sense of empathy for her (their to use gender correct pronouns; please see p.s. at end of review) because her situation doesn't improve and she doesn't change or go through an arc or learn a lesson. I haven't reached the end of this game, which certainly impacts my ability to critique this game, but I don't feel interested in this game, and don't care about this janitor, enough to try anymore.
I really, really wanted to enjoy this game but it feels draining, which I suppose is the point this game tries to make. But an important thing to consider, and to bring up "Papers, Please" again, is that you can have a great game around a seemingly bad or weird role to play. You just need to make sure its fun, and for "Diaries of a Spaceport Janitor", it just isn't.
P.S. there is a mechanic in this game where your character must change genders frequently. It's an interesting idea and I'm glad the devs included this sort of thing because it adds a unique spin to character, identity, plus I'd imagine the gender fluid community appreciates having a character that is relatable for once. My problem with this mechanic is that it is implemented very poorly in that it feels like you have no control over it, and it constantly sinks your money by happening, without fail, every 2-3 days. I don't find myself able to comment on this as I don't identify with the nonbinary or genderfluid community, so make of this mechanic and what it means for yourself.

The “Metroidvania” platformer enjoyed its heyday some 15-20 years ago when Super Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night ruled the roost, and eventually found their names lent to the genre’s title. While many games since then have borrowed the tried-and-true mechanics of these classics, Valdis Story: Abyssal City is one that does so while also re-creating the aesthetic of the old-school consoles — its colorful art style would feel right at home on a PlayStation. The hours of engaging gameplay at hand will especially satisfy the nostalgic.
In a world where demons and angels are at war, Wyatt and his crew set sail in order to track down his missing father. During the voyage, their ship is attacked by creatures from below and sunk. Beneath the water's surface, they find a slowly dying ancient city under constant attack from angels, demons and ferals. Separated from his crew, Wyatt must now reunite them while continuing the search for his father. During his journey, he discovers lost secrets and unravels mysteries surrounding him and his friends.
As with its classic inspirations, the bulk of the gameplay in Valdis Story is spent battling enemies and exploring the side-scrolling landscapes. The satisfaction of a good Metroidvania game is intact; you’ll come across many inaccessible doors and return to them hours later with a means of entry, filled with anticipation of what could be behind them. The location of your next task is not always obvious, with a vague line of text serving as the only clue. This lack of hand-holding might frustrate in other games, but it’s a boon to Valdis Story, as revisiting areas to more thoroughly explore only enhances the whole. Valdis Story rewards those who go out of their way to explore; a vital aspect of this Metroidvania-style game. As you leap around the beautiful 2D world, you acquire new equipment and spells that allow access to previously unreachable locations. Summoning ice pillars as temporary platforms, short-range teleports and wall-kicking are just a few of the abilities needed to fully traverse the city. Dozens of hidden items, chests and crew members wait to be found, some of which are extraordinarily hard to find, making it sweeter when you do.
There’s a solid progression system in place, injecting RPG aspects to great effect. Experience is earned through defeating enemies, with a substantial amount of unlockable skills and stat upgrades to choose from as each new player level is achieved. There’s even somewhat of a crafting mechanic — materials collected in the wild can be provided to vendors to increase the effectiveness of armor and weapons, or create new ones outright.
The combat in Valdis Story is fun. Stringing together combos with the aid of unlocked skills is enchanting from start to finish. Magic plays a major part, serving as a gratifying complement to melee swordplay. By the game’s conclusion, you’ll have access to a generous amount of spells ranging from elemental attacks, to stat buffs, to abilities that help you reach otherwise-inaccessible areas. The depth of combat comes to light most effectively while entrenched in the numerous boss fights. Some of these tests are quite stiff, particularly later in the game. Success comes through experimentation, practicing different spells on different bosses, and even exploring the area where the battle takes place. But if nothing’s working out, doubling back for some old-fashioned level grinding goes a long way.
Combat flows smoothly, and stringing attacks together is fast-paced and exciting. The keyboard controls are clunky, but they can be rearranged or a gamepad can be used. You can execute short-ranged dashes that allow you to dodge and move past foes, or employ more than twenty spells to deal damage, heal, boost your own abilities or reach new places. The sound effects that accompany them are appropriate, though a little artificial-sounding at times. Nevertheless, spell diversity is outstanding, and there are dozens of ways to approach combat in any particular battle. Often, you will need to mix up your strategy as some enemies focus on speed and manoeuvrability, while others are heavily armoured or stand back and shoot. There's a solid variety of foes, though their design relies on palette-swapping as the game progresses. On level up you can assign stat points and choose to focus on magic, melee or a mix of the two. It's a fun, flexible system that provides great variety on additional plays.
There are plenty of bosses to test your skills against, both story-based and optional, and you'll always need to be at your best to beat them. Monstrous armoured angels and sleek, agile demons are just a few you'll encounter. Different bosses require you to take down shields, stay above poisonous gas, navigate precarious platforms, destroy healing devices and even beat a time limit in order to destroy them. There's terrific variety, and, even on the normal difficulty setting, they are a real challenge to defeat. Once you do so, you are given a rank based on how soundly you thrashed them, and may be rewarded with extra experience or even additional stat or skill points to assign. At the end of the game you receive an overall ranking too, so completionists have a huge task ahead of them.
I had a wonderful time playing Valdis Story. Time and time again it exceeded my expectations, and it's a privilege that I was able to play and review it. Just when I thought I had seen the greatest boss or most intense challenge, it threw another one at me. One play through, as Wyatt, takes about 10-15 hours, so there's at least twice that to play as Reina and collect all the hidden items. Throw in Gilda and Vladyn, and you can double that play time again! As long as you're prepared for a challenging game, I can't recommend Valdis Story enough.

When I was a young boy, one of my favourite ways to waste time was with an old Warcraft 3 mod called "Elemental TD". Game was fantastic; take your good old fashioned Tower Defence game, but give em upgrade paths that change based on what elements you pick. You start off with a good old fashioned fire tower which would amount to good DPS with low damage over time, but then you could upgrade it with a water element with a steam tower that weakens enemies and does pure damage over time, OR you could upgrade it with the earth element for a LAVA tower, or you could upgrade it with the wind element for a BRUSHFIRE tower, or you could upgrade it with the light element for a FLARE tower. The possibilities were endless and it was always great fun playing around with each possibility, discovering new ones and seeing what worked best.
is a Rogue-like Binding of Isaac-style game that works off of exactly the same principle as Elemental TD; you start with a single element and as you play you pick up runes which you can combine to create new spells. If you think this sounds like a neat little idea for a gameplay element you are wrong because it is actually the most freaking incredible and flawlessly executed idea ever conceived and I am legitimately quite angry that it has taken THIS long for someone to put it into a game. You can stick with 2 different elements for all manner of projectile attacks, but later on you can get three-stage combiners to make spells from THREE different rune elements, allowing for literally hundreds of potential combinations. The game is pretty unforgiving with it's bullet-hell challenge but as you learn more spells you become better equipped to handle it.
If you die in Runers, true to the Rogue-like genre you are forced to start again with nothing, however you do get to keep the knowledge of potential spell combinations in your 'runedex', easing the challenge more by arming you with knowledge rather than stat increases. You also don't need combiners for spells you have already discovered (though the game wont actually TELL you this). This is a very rewarding way for players to feel like they're making progress, knowing they have to figure out the best possible combinations of spells rather than just being able to brute force through every level with basic spells... well.... I'm sure that was the idea, anyway, as it all sort of gets ruined by the chaos rune.
When you start a game you pick a race, a profession and a starting rune, the race and profession are inconsequential and  differ depending on your own playstyle, and starting spells are spammable, each having anywhere between a 0.2 and 0.5 second cooldown and either a 0.1 or 0.2 second GLOBAL cooldown. The global cooldown is in place to prevent players from putting base spells on all of their mouse buttons and spamming like crazy, since each individual spell has its own cooldown. Chaos, however, does not give a sh*t. With it's 0.2 second cooldown and 0.1 second global, if you happen to find a second chaos rune in the first few levels you can put one on each mouse button, hold them both down and glide through the first 5 levels machine-gunning everything you see. It is undoubtedly an optimal strategy but I guess I cant fault the game because it took me a while to figure it out, by which time I had already figured out a good portion of the game.
See there are two ways to play runers; the way where you jump on the wiki immediately to find out what all the most powerful spells are, or the way where you play for 10 minutes and fail spectacularly before going on the wiki to find out what all the most powerful spells are. In all seriousness though I had full intention of getting through this game and unlocking all the spells without cheating but I cracked when I used three upgraded runes, prepared to use the ultimate spell of creature destruction and was given a soggy weet-bix cannon with a 30 second cooldown. The game became significantly less fun after I had this knowledge though, so I implore you to play for as long as possible before resorting to this.
My one major complaint with the game is in the spells. Some of the spells are really fun; you can shoot, use force pushes, gravity, sound powers, stun powers, speed boosts for yourself, there is a telefrag spell, and yes there is at least one super-powered nuke spell which kills everything near you. I feel they did not make the most of the medium, however, and copped out on a LOT of potential. Some spells are just pathetic as well, especially for spells that cost three runes and extremely rare 3-stage combiners to make. I seem to recall there being an ultimate ability that did nothing but move the creatures around a bit and change the direction of missiles slightly, but not enough so that they don't hit you. There was also a dark rain spell that slowed and did damage over time to a certain area that was so small it never did /anything/. When you unearth a flop spell you generally just chuck it immediately, putting a little cross next to the spell in your runedex so you never craft it again, and it's possible that some spells were meant to be useless; like I'm sure there is a spell in the world of Harry Potter that can only be used by the top wizards of the world that does nothing but turn bread into spiders or something. It just sucks when you waste an entire run getting the resources to craft a single ultimate spell only to have it be a move that drops fluffy marshmallows where your cursor is.
Also the link between the spell you get and the elements used is beyond tenuous for the mostpart. Dark, light and wind = sleep spell? I mean... yeah, okay... I mean I probably would /not/ have been able to think of much better for that specific spell slot but some of them really are a reach.
Runers has a few flaws, but none are in the gameplay. I actually think this is as solid a game as you can get from an indie developer; gameplay is fun, replay value is INSANE and there is always something new to explore. Runers is one of the most fun rogue-likes I have ever played, and I forgive any shortcomings it may have.

The main strength of Runers would have to be the spell crafting system.  You collect random runes and combine them to make different spells and to improve spells you already have.  Each spell was designed individually, so you can't guess what a certain combination of runes will make until you try it.  There is a total of 285 spells to discover, so that alone can keep you busy for a while.  The spell variety includes different buffs, debuffs, beams, projectiles, AoE, things which effect an entire room, and special utilities.  There is also incentive to discover spells since you don't need to use any combiners to make a spell you already discovered by making it.  It is the only feature which makes future playthroughs easier.  Other than that, you unlock more difficulties and a passive and active ability to start with by making it to the end.  Music, sounds, and visuals are nice, and there is a fair amount of enemy variety.  The bosses you fight in each playthrough aren't even the same most of the time.
The issues are a few bugs which sometimes cause the game to crash, a few typos, and secrets being extremely rare drops from bosses.  The developers also seem to have stopped supporting the game.
I would suggest this game to anyone who likes rogue-lites and enjoys discovering beautiful spells and possibly to people who like danmaku.

Runers is a game a few steps from greatness.
That is to say, the ideas inside are interesting and in some cases rather innovative and cool, but are hampered by mechanics or a simple lack of polish. Essentially, Runers is a roguelike twinstick shooter with heavy twitch elements - think like Binding of Isaac and Nuclear Throne - and also a surprisingly deep level of RPG elements.
To jump into the nitty-gritty: You're a Runer, an individual who uses the power of, well, runes, to create and cast spells. The basic runes are all immediately available as starting spells. You can discover more by combining two runes or three runes, the number of runes generally denoting complexity of the spell at hand. Runes, which are picked up as loot, also sometimes have modifies to the spell they make, like making the bullets larger or last longer or deal more damage and so on, and are also used to enhance spells you already have. It's an interesting system, which is heavily hampered by the system that is attatched: Combiners.
Combiners are pieces of loot you can pick up as well. When you start the game, you know all the basic spells (one rune spells) but none of the others. If you don't know a spell (combined it previously, in this or previous playthroughs) you need a combiner to make it. If it's a three-rune spell, you need to either find a triple combiner or make one from four combiners. This is compounded by the fact that Combiners are somewhat rare - the only time they drop, gaurenteed, is from bosses, who drop triples on death.
This slows the sense of progress and discover immensely, for better or worse. It should also be noted that the game has great documentation inside it for the spells you've made, with great sorting options, that even allow you to preview some elements of the spell you're about to make (For example, you'll be able to sort your Undiscovered, Creatable spells by, say, Buffs, or other categories). The good side of this is that your discovers cross playthroughs, leading to a real feeling of accomplishment once you don't need those pesky combiners as much.
The starting options are surprisingly vairied, with each race having clear playstyles and each class synergizing or shoring up the weaknesses of your race. The combinations of those and your starting spell tends to define a run, for better or worse, lending replayability.
The game is divided into individual floors, and each floor into rooms. Rooms generally harbor enemies, a bunch of destructable objects, both, or an event, plus a possible aura (which affects one or more of your stats). Events are puzzles or situations you can choose to activate for a piece of loot or a permanent buff to one of your stats. When you access the stairs for the first time on a floor, you get another free item or upgrade as well, and when you kill enough enemies, you level up and gain a perk.
Personally, I found the perks to be a bit situational and also in short supply in addition. It's unfortunate, but I kept running into the same perks repeatedly.
Enemies range from simple to fight to being confusing and incomprehensible. Mos memorable is the experience of wandering into a room to be stunned and then trapped by a swarm of melee enemies, against whom I had no recourse. Such a situation, while rare, still happens often enough to be worth comment.
Bosses, who occur once every three floors, serve as a sort of set piece and battles that benchmark your abilities. Each one has tactics that work better or worse, I can honestly say you need a variety of spells to truly succeed. Though, some spells have a lot of use and utility.
In closing, I would hesitantly reccomend Runers, with the caveat that it's not that great at first blush. It does, however, eventually grow into something rather unique and engaging.

2 button controls - thrust and fire. For the most part you are automatically moving forward, there is no back or stop unless you count rocks and scenery. Timing is everything or you bang into enemies, gas clouds and many other things that will kill you, some being quite hard to see against the background.
Some levels have you in a turret position and all you have to do is shoot, these levels are too easy and ultimately dull.

The whole thing felt more like a mobile app game.
After finishing a few levels and getting used to the controls, I made myself a drink and completely forgot I was playing it. I feel no draw to complete it.

Castlestorm--Part RTS, part arcade figthing game, part Angry Birds style castle breaking action, and all fun.
The basic gameplay has you with your castle (which you can build and upgrade yoursefl) facing an opposing castle.  You can either knock it down or capture it flag, and you can use the ballista, your soldiers, or your hero, or a combination of all three.  Using one means you aren't using the others, though, so picking which one works for you and when is a large part of the gameplay.
Add in some silly humor and cartoonish graphics and you have a very fun, very inexpensive game.

The Good:

The Bad:

Love Metroidvania?  Join the club.  Valdis Story is currently easily my favorite of the PC Metroidvanias I've played in recent years.  It features excellent, tight combat mechanics that feel somewhat like Devil May Cry thanks to the mobility and attack options from the game's spell system.  The world is mostly a joy to explore and new travel skills are given at just the right pace to keep the player interested in exploring more.  Furthermore, there are two characters (with two more upcoming, but in very slow development) and some impactful storyline changes that can add a lot to the replayability of the game.
One of my main complaints about the game is the lack of enemy diversity,  It's not a huge issue, and the game does change it up by giving existing enemies new abilities as you level up, but one of my favorite things about Castlevania SOTN was that just about every zone had its unique monsters that each added to the atmosphere of the zone.  In this game, it just feels like you're fighting those angelic monk dudes all the time except in different places.  Also, the game has a number of difficult platforming sections which can be very frustrating to some players.  Thankfully, not all of them are required.
Fantastic game.  Very easy to learn with a helpful interface, but still with challenging AI and scenarios.

I'm not really good at writing reviews but, because this game is worth it, i decided to do so:
-What is it?
-It's an sandbox strategy game, where you design your ships and capture zones to win (simple, right?)
-What are the gamemodes?
-Singleplayer, Multiplayer and Challenges
-What is the goal of the game?
-You have a galactic to conquer, bosses to defeat and chalanges to complet (also you can dominate other players in multiplayer, if you so desire)
-Why is it so special for me?
-I'm not a huge strategy games fan, but I'm doing well in this game. Why? Because the game allows me to create my own crazy tactics, units and it doesn't punish me if I fail. Instead, I can adapt myself to the situation, try a different tactic (like zerg rush, or (selfmade) boss run) without even restarting the level. I've never seen such a high level of flexibility in a strategy game
-Other pros?
-The graphic are nice and simple, the AI is surprisingly good written, which makes every win satisfying (especially the boss fights), you don't need to PAY 2 ENJOY the game, and there is NO GAMBLING! (more and more F2P games are based just on that to maximise the profit, which hurts the name of that title)
-Cons?
-You cannot rotate the parts, and the mirror line should work like in other sandbox games (Robocraft, Space Engeneers etc.)
Long story short - just try out this game, it's worth it.

TL;DR - DON'T PLAY THE GAME IF YOU'RE PHOTOSENSATIVE
I so badly wanted to enjoy this game. I played for about 2 hours, (~9 ingame days) before having to stop. It wasn't that the game was bad in terms of gameplay, (I actually really liked just wandering around the world and seeing everything), but that it's currently a buggy and literally painful mess.
Currently, there's bugs that caused me to have physical headaches due to some visuals in the game. In the game, there's a very clever use of Z-Fighting to simulate flickering screens, which are plentiful around the world. However, the primary colours of these screens are Cyan and Red, which are inverse colours of eachother. There IS an option to turn the screens off so that they're just Cyan, BUT there's three bugs in place that ruin this option:
1 - There are these stations around the world that you need to frequently visit to stop your screen from distorting and to help text be legible, (the effect itself isn't that bad, and the items you need to buy from the stations are fairly cheap). These stations use the Cyan-Red flashing screens, and WILL NOT change no matter the setting you have set.
2 - Your own home, the place you start and end every day in, has the flashing screens, and won't change no matter what setting you have your visuals set to.
3 - EVERYTIME you leave your home, your visuals get reset to default, which means everything's turned off, which means all those flashing screens are flashing again, even if you've kept the game on.
Outside of the photosensative bugs, your sound settings get reset every time you start up the game, so the music and sound effects blast in your ear every time you start up the game.
There's also no clock or map in the game itself, (there's a manual that's included in the download that has a map included), but personally I didn't find it that bad, since there are arrows on the ground to help show where districts are. However, I know that could be a problem for some.
The one thing I do like are the visuals, and just the look to the whole port. It kinda weirdly feels familiar yet very alien, and it's why I had bought the game in the first place. And honestly, if it wasn't for the headache-enducing bugs that the devs don't seem to want to address, I would honestly recommend it on the looks alone, (though only when it's on sale, since I don't think it's worth the $10 price tag it usually has).
I'd really want to recommend this game, but until the bugs with the screens get fixed/changed, I can't honestly recommend this to anyone, simply for their health and saftey.

This is an action-platformer in the style of new
games.
There are a few key differences, however. Unlike
, this game emphasizes quality over quantity when it comes to item drops and spells. Enemies drop crafting ingredients, not gold or items. Each character has only a handful of armors and weapons, and every one caters to a different playstyle and has multiple upgrade levels.
The gameplay is more akin to a fighting game (especially in boss battles). There is a heavy emphasis on dodging over blocking. Striking enemies at opportune moments is much more important than simply hitting them as much as possible. You do have a revive built into your abilities, but you are still fairly fragile.
This is much easier to play than a fighting game, though. Your skill cancel is a simple press of the down key, and dodging is just pressing left or right after that. Your assist has its own button, and spell casting and super mode have modifier keys. The game offers some tutorials, but muscle memory is the only real stumbling block here.
Boss battles emphasize pattern recognition and reaction time over button mashing, and since your skill cancels have a short cooldown, spamming will get you nowhere. Killing a tricky boss after spending four lives learning their patterns is a very satisfying feeling. Retries are unlimited and place you right in the boss room, but its still crucial to keep your cool and respond to attacks carefully.
There are downsides, of course. Whenever the game chooses to focus on platforming over combat, it becomes significantly less fun. Thankfully most of the timed platforming challenges are optional, though you will be missing out on a few items if you ignore them, as I chose to.
Like any non-linear game, there are times when you will be unsure where to go, or where you accidentally miss important things because the game doesn't tell you enough. This is compounded by some occasionally suspect level design, particularly areas where it's easy to fall down several rooms and be forced to repeat an area, or where enemies can stunlock or toss you easily.
The map and menus are rather bland. While it has some nice sprite work, the graphics options don't really give everything room to shine. It also doesn't scale well, so if (like me) you have a fairly large monitor and play in fullscreen, the upscaling is very noticable.
The story is nothing exciting. Like
, it's mostly relegated to text boxes whenever you find a new area or kill a boss. It has a few engaging reveals and some pleasant backstory here and there, but the story is not a reason alone to play this game.
Ultimately, this game doesn't hold your hand, but it has a reasonable difficulty curve and skill floor. It expects you to work a little bit for your victories, but it is neither impossible nor unfair. If you like action platformers and skill-based combat, look no further. Just be sure to use a controller.

I have just short of 5 hours in game time as of writing this. I think this is the best offering of card games that are inspired by MtG, and I've played many. There are only a few changes and additions to the game mechanics here, but they are critical to making this a better game.
The creature speed ratings is really cool - some slow but hard hitting creatures can devastate your opponent, unless he manages to get out faster creatures that your slow poke can't block or directly attack. Faster creatures give more flexability but are generally less powerful.
The Shrines for mana is nice too. You can play them for a "level up" in that color, which is functionally similar to a spell that requires more than one of a mana color to cast. Or you can spend it for +1 mana which is functionally similar to a basic land in MtG, but here it also gives you a card draw. It includes the chance to have a resource advantage without the 'mana screw' that can really ruin an otherwise fun game of MtG. Keeping this system in play means you still need to make decisions about your mana base in deckbuilding; you can try to run slim and get more utility cards in your deck, but you are putting yourself at resource risk.
But hey, it is FREE and has lots of good content at 100% free. I've not spent a dime on the game and I'm not anywhere near a pay wall, and having lots of fun. So just download it and find out for yourself!

The
functions similar to MtG, but with a few twists. You can directly target your opponents creatures with attacks. However each creature has a speed stat, ranging from 1 to 4, in addition to health and attack. A creature can only ever attack or block a creature with the same or lower speed. A higher speed means more flexibility in combat but comes at the price of lower stats or higher cost.
Creatures can move freely between a front and support line (except when they have previously attacked this turn). While a creature is protected from attacks in the support line, it also can't attack or block itsself, which makes it the perfect place for small creatures with key effects. This game is
. You don't have to spend a dime and you can still build a competitive deck in about a week with semi-casual play. As you play you automatically unlock new starter decks and the corresponding faction's quest zones. From unlocking all zones alone you get multiple rares (second highest rarity) and one epic (highest rarity) of every faction. Every 8 hours a variety of quests spawn in one faction zone from which you can choose one. Rewards range from small amounts of gold, a few common or uncommon cards or small packs (4 cards) to 12 pack boxes, rare and epic cards (no duplicates) or premium currency. There's also the academy, which gives you a really good quest once every 3 days.
In the draft mode Trials, which you can enter for a fee, you break even after 3 wins (50% win rate) and at the max of 10 wins you get rewards, which are worth more than 7 times the entry fee (including 5 packs).
For those who want to spend a few bucks there are custom card backs or premium packs, which have higher chances for epics and will not give you cards you already have 4 of (max number which can be included in a deck).

While many wait for the next big title, smaller indie games fill the gaps within the major AAA releases. Among these titles is Nidhogg from developer Messhof. At first glance the portrait displayed isn't anything that would take a spot in a respectable museum but take another look and the fine details may surprise you. Nidhogg's image may not be of this generation or the last few for that matter but for all it's simplicity does its transcend to the height of AAA titles?
Focused on it's combat Nidhogg offers very little in content, the single player consists of dueling several enemies within the four available stages in side-scrolling fashion. The goal is the same throughout, make it across to the opposite end whist in numerous duels of death. The respawns are unlimited but once either makes it across 3 screens the game is over and the victor is eaten by the Nidhogg, the world tree chomping worm of Norse mythology.
If there is anything that Nidhogg does extremely well is its combat, the intricate system requires quick reflexes, perfect timing and finesse. Considering the simple premise, the multitude of stances and moves offer up a good amount of depth.  Duels expanding across the pixilated canvas aren't uncommon and it's a testament to how deep the combat is. Stage hazards do play their role but in the end the better fighter will come out on top. It's any easy game to get into and one that offers up some intense moments with duels reaching ridiculous heights.
Without a doubt the visuals of Nidhogg are not the main attraction, it's sprite based aesthetics do enough to portray the environments and figures throughout the world. Though limited the end result gives Nidhogg some visual charm and identity. Seeing the floor and walls painted with the players matter is chuckle worthy and a nice touch displaying the chaos among adversaries.
However, the small amount of stages leaves much to desire, considering how simple the levels are it's hard to imagine why any DLC has not been introduced. Stages present little in the imagination department with minimal inspiration. In light of how much was presented in the combat one would imagine a larger emphasis in the level design to promote replayability.
Nidhogg's multiplayer is crippled by the absence of any online lobby system that could in fact strengthen the competitive mode drastically. The limited online mutliplayer consist of single encounters unless played locally via the bracket based tournament mode. The idea behind the mode is brilliant but why it isn't available online is a major misstep in the design.
Nidhogg is a charming experience that could of been greater if not for it's lack in content and multiplayer options. The simple to execute yet deep combat system is offset by many other flaws in design. Nidhoggs first attempt has the most important aspect of any game of this style right, it may be completely lacking in narrative but definitely a game made for competitive multiplayer. Playing with some buds is fun and Nidhogg does a great job with contact kills allowing you to embellish every neck break or impalement of a friend.  It's simple, stupid, and addicting fun.  Pick it up on a sale, the asking price might be a bit steep for the short but humorous experience.
+Great Combat
+Unique Identity
+The Nidhogg has no Mercy
-Lack of online options and lobbies
-Cloud stage is weak
-Lag can be an issue
-Flat soundtrack

Look's like one of the decent fast paced shooter, so far, it's ain't that bad, graphics are similar to source, variety of classes to choose from and two different kind of zombies, heavy and the weaklings.
Four maps to play with, it should worth your time and it's usually fun to play with friends. Start with some laughter and intense if it gets on when hell break loose.
Classes to choose are
1) Pointman - Usually one of the close-quater class that is armed with a auto shotgun, with his sidearm as a duel handgun. Usually his main equipment is a grenade.
2) Support - One of the weakest class yet he can support the others with ammo and equipment supply in case they have run out which is usually rarely, his armed with an SMG yet it does a pretty low damage. One of the basic pistol and his equipment which looks similar to the ammo crate from Half Life 2.
3) Assault - A heavily armed unit, carrying a galil as his main type of wep, yet he can be slow sometimes though he's quite one of the tanks among the classes around here, same sidearm as the support. Same equipment as the Pointman which is a grenade. If you're looking for an assault rifle class to play, then this is yours.
4) Technician - One of my favourite class to play actually, he's able to spawn a turret which is similar to those Combine Turrets in Half Life 2. It can be used as a distraction to zombies and sure this class does a high dps among the others if used correctly. Without his turret, he can be quite useless excluding his pump shotgun which should be easy enough to one shot kill the infected in the head. Armed with a pistol and like I said, a turret. Don't lose the turret, used it as a good distraction if you're happen to be swarm.
5) Finally we have our, Sniper, quite a devastating class since he wield a sniper rifle enough to penetrate the bodies of the infected. Though if he's swarmed, he still have an incendiary grenade which is enough to start an AOE (Area of Effect) Damage towards the infected that stands in it. Doesn't really team-damage the other class nor him, if you're looking for an AOE Class, then this should be your favourite then. Armed with a pistol, similar kind to the other classes.
Usually the objective is simple, breach in a territory that is filled with infected, plant the bomb and get the hell out of here before it explodes. Do you have a phrase saying, "Are we rushing in, or we are going sneaky beaky like"? It's usually all about rushing in so don't bother checking some of the rooms, there's nothing inside anyways but zombies if possible.
I have nothing wrong the bots as they did their job pretty well but except for them, struggling to get themselves inside, for example, one of those escape route, like the elevator, then the vehicle. So just leave them behind to their death or try to save them, it's your decision to make, choose wisely.
So far, I would rate this game, 7/10, one of the best fast-paced game, I've ever played though it could use some improvement including more kind of infected rather than the Heavy, Fast and the Slow.

This game is pretty nice. It seems to hit the sweet spot between not overly complicated, and being deep enough for a very nice game. This isn't a kiddy game though; there is a learning curve, but it's really fun as you do so. (I also played the demo before this.) You can choose any country on the map as well. The game is challenging, but not over the top hard. I love this game so far.
The gameplay seems quick as well. You don't have to wait for 500 other civilizations to move 1 troop at a time. To me this is a big plus. And yet countries are all doing their own thing creating blocs, declaring war, proposing things at the UN (if they are a member = in top 12 in GDP), etc.
For the research/tech tree there are a lot of options. Some countries start with higher military tech, econonomical tech, etc. It's pretty cool. You can create your own stock market and add countries to it which increases income. There is also loans/debt, and you can pay them back as you see fit. You can eventually go bankrupt, but you can improve your technology/economy via research.
If you ever played the board game Risk, the military aspect of managing war is like that in many ways. You use different military actions in battle that have chances of success, you can see your troop numbers, can assign as many units as you want in the battle, and add more units as you fight through re-inforcements once they are produced (takes some time). It's pretty cool. You don't have to go all over the map manage individual units. You won't see your units, but in each battle it shows the number of soldiers, tanks, planes, etc. you have. You can also automate battels if you choose. There is also a number of options for espionage, influencing democracy, etc. Countries do attack one another, but it seems pretty balances so far. I love all the interaction.
There is a UN. It consists of the top 12 countries in GDP which can change over time.. It's done nicely because those countries that declare war a lot also get a vote. ;) At the UN countries can create proposals and they need a certain percentage of countries to approve it. It's really nice, and what's awesome is it's not just you making proposals.. there are some good ones that make since that others propose. In one war I defeated Russia in a battle which means I can choose to reduce their army for a while, liberate certain provinces, or take over certain provinces. They can deny the proposal as well; each province is worth a certain score up to 100, so lets say province 1 & 2 are worth 90 points.. Russia would probably accept that because it's less than 100. Pretty awesome.. Even when you win, both sides have to agree on the peace treaty, or you can propose another treaty, or attack another area I believe as well.. Awesome.
You can start your own block just by inviting others to join your block. A lot of countries will turn down your offer, but you have ways of improving relations. Some still seem to never want to join, but that is pretty realistic. There also are options for your bloc. Countries can come and go in the bloc, so you have to maintain relations as well.
I have encountered one bug so far, and it has to deal with resources. It's a pretty big bug as you get negative resources which means you can't build tanks, etc. later in the game. The workaround suppossidely is to turn off imports/exports before proposing the peace treaty; the problem is it's easy to forget this.
I definitely recommend this if you like these types of games. Keep in mind it'd not a clone of military management games. This is pretty unique, but it seems done just right. This will be one of my favorites. :) I've played 2-3 games so far, and each game was a little different. Some countries are more aggressive, but each game has had countries doing things a little differently so far. This game has only been out a little while, and I've already played 32+ hours. :)

A rather fun and engaging Grand-Strategy-Lite game from 3-man indie team Jujubee.

That said, for someone like myself who enjoys the complexities of the genre, this is actually an enjoyable, more casual experience that is still fun. For those looking to get a taste of either these experiences, I can most certainly recommend it.
That said, more elements, scenarios, and gameplay additions would be welcome to pad the game out a little more. There's a great foundation just asking to be worked upon, so I do hope the developers use this potential moving forward and gives Realpolitiks the extra post-release support it deserves!

The story continues right after the first game and is built to reuse a lot of old assets(characters, maps, ...). I usually wouldn't mind about the story in general, but every character just acts unusual. It's not at all convincing how they act/react. An example:
However the gameplay itself is anything but great, too. The first monsters you encounter are pretty tough, so you might just level up a bit. TL:DR, If you enjoy realistic games, and you enjoy RTS games, this is great even if you pay full price
First off, if you played earlier men of wars and found the to be overly difficult and annoying, this fixes problems. I remember playing MoW Vietnam. The final kill counts were like me 600 kills, them 6. This game is NOT like that. They allow for a lot more renforcements which creates bigger and better battles.
If you have never played, Imagine Company of Heroes but way more realistic. Every unit has an inventory which can be scavanged and depleted. If you have a tank in battle for a prolonged ammount of time you may find your self out of HE, AP, or the covited APCR(I will expand on ammo types and options in the next section). Machine guns can run black, and so can snipers. Every one is prone to running completely black on ammo. The cool thing is you can always scavange, many times in my American play I found myself picking up and MP40 when I felt like it may be more effective for the close range fighting that was happening. All weapons and all ammo drops when units die, and can be picked up, unless the unit is blown up. The game also allows you to buy a supply truck completely loaded with 1000s of rounds of ammo.
Also each unit has many options as to weapons they can use, unlike CoH, you can actually have unit switch to a side arm, or switch to grenade, you have so much more control of each man on the field. Where this become most evident it with the armor, This game has some of the best tank physics I have ever seen, when you shoot something with an AP round, you can actually see the hole if it punctures, as well as it hits every on in its path just like a real AP round. It does not just blow up the tank, it blows a hole through it. That is if you actually get a clean hit with a big enough cannon. This is the best part of this game, tank on tank battles. I had a single Stuart take on anything the Jap army could send, That same tank was completly worthless against the germans. Super realistic and fun, and allows for complete control.
My last point and best part about this game, is the direct control. If you just hit E on any unit it gives you complete control. You aim the weapon, fire it, and move with the WASD. Where as normally in an RTS you just right click to attack, in this you can move and attack, with the most possible control, especially with tanks. Moving into postion with a sherman and hitting a Panzer IV point blank with a 76mm APCR Is one of the coolest things you can do.
From a game play standpoint, I got the whole thing on sale, with all the DLC. Which comes with 5 mission for each of the Russian, German, American, Japanese, and Common Wealth factions. Play slow and enjoying it took me 8 hours to beat the USA campagn. So a lot of paytime there. TONS of units!!

The human mind has an innate ability to organize memories into stories... and then ask if someone else is authoring the story instead. Stories within stories and their authors inside them are common themes in various metafictional novels and films but have not appeared very often in games. Memoria builds an interesting, labyrinthian tale from themes of imagination, memory and myth that pleases the senses as well as the mind.
Memoria picks up where Chains of Satinav left off, with the bird-catcher Geron once again leading the cast. Since playing the previous title is all but necessary I will not discuss any plot details from either. As a general description it can be said that the story takes place in two completely different times and places and accordingly on two different levels which mix in various interesting ways as events unfold. Unfortunately the story inside the main story, the one detailing Sadja, a princess in an Arabian-like kingdom, begins on the wrong foot. I have rarely seen a more cold-blooded and merciless exposition beginning to a story as the one for Sadja. To make things even worse her quest is a rather abstract one making it difficult to become immediately involved. Sadja herself is odd company: ambitious to the brink of ruthlessness with an odd sense of a grand fate awaiting her. As such she is as unusual creative choice but in the end does fit into the overall themes and design.
The writing in general is more concerned with the whole than the parts which I found pleasing. There are no quotable one-liners nor amusing banter but given the fairytale surroundings this austerity may indeed be better than any rhetorical flower arrangements. The somewhat weak beginning is the only major flaw and offset by the very impressive ending. The many layers of mythology logic seen throughout the story are also unusual and take the place of any everyday realism. In this case the high fantasy works since the whole is kept to an economical length are there are no larger-than-life emotional outbursts.
While the writing takes some time to draw the player in this cannot be said from the sensory stimulation. The hand-drawn environments are both lucid and vivid and could not have been done better. One of the key strengths with Chains of Satinav was the bittersweet orchestral soundtrack and while Memoria does not reach the same heights it does an admirable job of setting the mood. A true weakness in the presentation are once again the animations. Slight ruggedness during adventures is somewhat easy to ignore but becomes difficult indeed during moments of dialogue. When the only part of the face moving is the mouth the effect is jarring to say the least.
As the puzzles require fantasy logic to solve some of them may be problematic but I did not see any insurmountable ones. The number of items, hotspots and screens needed for a major puzzle are kept to reasonable limits. The game also has a questlog to remind you of the current task as well as lore reminders of the things you have learned. Should you lose hope on a puzzle there is even a hint system for the desperate. Chains of Satinav introduced limited spellcasting into the otherwise traditional pointing-and-clicking. Geron only had one ability at his disposal in that game but now he has two in addition to Sadja's three. Not all of these are used very much so some editing could have been useful but on the other hand this system lessens the clunky "bottomless pockets" inventory-based problems of many other adventure games.
Memoria's ultimate strength is perhaps a strong sense of identity. The developers did their very best with the indie resources available and cleary love the genre and the game as much as the adventure game audience does. Memoria will not conquer the world any more than any other contemporary adventure will but for those willing to appreciate its quiet appeal there is much pleasure to be discovered within these ten hours.

Short version:
+ 16bit Anime style
+ Nice 8bit-like soundtrack
+ Different characters with uniqe abilities
+ Level system
+ Unlockable characters with more abilites and more leveling fun
+ Local Multiplayer
+ Online Multiplayer
+ Just having fun with mindlessly beating the ♥♦♣♠ out of everyone who dares to cross your way
- Level is capped to 50 without DLC (with DLC max 99)
- Online Multiplayer sometimes desynchs as of now.
- Camera lock in local Co-Op. Mode (If 2 Players are going too far away the camera will lock and enemies can get knocked out of the camera wich means that you can't hit them until they're back on screen. This does not happen in online Co-Op.)
- No CPU players in Battle Grounds Mode
Phantom Breaker: Battle Grounds
is a anime beat em' up in the style of the 16bit-era with sweet 8bit-like soundtrack. You start with one of the 4 different characters. Each of those have their own abilities. As you go on in the game your character will gain exp and level up wich makes this game really addictive, since you want to max out your character and want to be able to play on harder difficulties and beat more ♥♦♣♠ out of your enemies. Well at least these were your thoughts but unfortunally without the DLC your level is capped at 50 instead of the maximum 99. Talking about the level system: you collect red crystals from defeated enemies. At the end of each round your exp will be count together and you might level up if you collect enough of these. With each level up you will obtain skill points for your character wich you can add on either abilities or on the stats like attack, defence and speed. With the level cap of 50 you will be only able to get 250 skill points wich is barely enough to unlock all skills and boost 5 (from 30) stats. But on LV99 you sometimes feel a little OP and so you can always remove abilites and stats and make unused skillpoints. You can even reset the playerstats and abilities (but not the level) and make this game a little bit more challenging. The Multiplayer modes are also a lot of fun
(Online Co-Op is added now, read update below). The Co-Op mode let's you play the game with up to 4 players at once. However I have a really really big issue with the Co-Op mode's camera: If 2 Players are going too far away the camera will lock and enemies can get knocked out of the camera wich means that you can't hit them until they're back on screen. This is so obnoxious if you have a high combo going on and need to cancel this out because of this! At least the coud make the Camera Zoom out like in SSB-Series if players are going too far away from each other. The Battle Ground mode let's you play VS against your friends to duke it out who really is the best brawler in this game. Just make sure that each of the characters have the same ammount of skillpoints used to make it a fair battle or handycap yourself until you get to your limits. The only thing missing there are CPU players for either practicing or just add more fun to the mess.
CO-OP UPDATE:
So the devs have released a netplay code for this game. Now you can play either Co-Op mode or Battle Grounds mode with up to four players online. It works quite well and you also don't have to deal with the locked camera anymore. This gives you and your friends a lot more freedom and features way better cooperative play. However, it does lose synchronisation some times, and once it does so it will never get back synchronised leading all players to go back to the main menu. This is quite annoying when this happens as you have to replay the stage from the beginning. It also once happened that one of my friends camera was locked onto my character instead of his own character making just it a BIT akward to play for him ;P. But other than that the rest of the online play feature is pretty stable and does things right.
Conclusion: If you want to revisit the old 16bit beat em' up series or like anime or even both this game is just for you. Be aware that a gamepad is recomanded for this game since the keyboard controlls are a little bit ♥♦♣♠ed up and you cant re-align them like you want to have them...

Okay so I beat the game. Took my 10 hours (because I got stuck a few times. I enjoyed it a lot! Time for a short review.
What's the best thing about the game? Well it would have to be, obviously, the art. All the areas areas to explore are simply gorgeous to look at, and most of it is interactive (main character will at least comment on things you look at).
What's the worst thing about the game? The puzzles are VERY contrived. So many times I got stuck simply because the answer to a puzzle is so difficult to figure out. I had to use a walkthrough after hitting brick walls, but I don't regret it as it allowed me to delve further into the interesting story and awesome visuals.
Example of contrived puzzle : to find a gem, one has to pour wine into a mold, do a service for a mage hidden in a library (seriously, you only see his shadow), find out he can solidify things, then have him solidify the wine. I had no clue that I could use the wine for that. There's also a maze (I HATE MAZES) but THANKFULLY you can skip it after enough time has elapsed (after getting lost). And the end is, to not spoil anything, just strange.
What's okay? The voice acting is well done, ESPECIALLY the talking staff. Music is... forgettable but it fits, controls work very well and the magic spells gives a nice twist to gameplay, though it is underused in my opinion.
Is it worth it? Yeah! Absolutely. If you can forgive yourself for using a walkthrough and just enjoy the story. Seriously, the puzzles are just a headache otherwise. Some parts can be done without one though.
However, I recommend playing the first game first, as it is a direct sequel and many things in this game will be unclear otherwise (why is the fairy turned into a raven?). I didn't play the first game, but I regret it.
Chains of Satinav, get that one first.

Before reading this review, please note that this is an early access game, and will subject to change as it further develops.
I've been waiting for this game for quite some time when I first saw the game on Greenlight back in December of 2014. It's an extremely good, and addicting game. I've met some really cool people who really make the game fun to play. The only issues I have with the game currently, is lack of players (just came out), and a few bugs (nothing too major.)
The game takes a lot of influence from Garry's Mod Trouble in Terrorist town, where you have 3 classes; Detective, Innocent, and the Traitors. This game has 4; Bloodhound (essentially like the Detective), Innocent, Murder (like the Traitors), and Vampires. The object is the same; track down, and deduce who the murders are. However, as a murder you can become a vampire, and infect others so that they too can become Vampires, creating your whole army of Vampires.
As an innocent, you really need to stick with the bloodhounds (detectives) to try and track down the murders.  The bloodhounds can use a DNA scanner to try and match who the killer is with the victim's corpse, or can even use a seance to talk with the dead to gain information about who the culprit is. The murder is by far the most fun to play as. Lie and decieve is your game, and with many tools/weapons in your arsenal, it's an absolute blast to lie and stab your way to victory.
You'll need to collect coins spread out throughout the manor, and in some objects, to be able to purchase weapons, teleporters, and other tools at your disposal. Keep in mind, each class has a different loadout out, e.x. a murder can purchase a flamethrower, but a innocent can't.
For the price of $5.49 in it's current state, I highly recommend this game. I've put in almost 7 hours, and I'm still having an absolute blast playing this game, and learning more about the game.
With a great, and active community, I can only see this game getting better.
